Contributors

About the author

Eickhel Mendoza is a Microsoft Business Applications MVP with many years of experience in

project management, Microsoft Azure development, and Microsoft Power Platform technologies.

He is a team lead of the Business Apps department and oversees all Microsoft 365 and Power

Platform projects. He has contributed to significant community events such as the Power Plat-

form World Tour, Global Azure Bootcamp, Microsoft 365 Developer Bootcamp, and Dynamics

365 Saturdays.

He coordinates the TenerifeDev and Power Platform Canarias user groups with a group of

like-minded developers eager to share their knowledge in different technologies. Eickhel is also

a member of the organizing committee of the Business Applications Summit Spain.

I want to express my gratitude to all the individuals who have influenced my passion for technology: my

parents Numa and Yenny, my teachers, my colleagues, and Osvaldo, who have consistently motivated me to

create great things.

About the reviewers

Yves Habersaat is a business applications consultant and AI tech lead at Sword Group in Swit-

zerland, specializing in building applications and solutions with Microsoft 365, Azure, Dynamics

365, and the Power Platform.

With a passion for modern development technologies and application lifecycles, Yves focuses

on Microsoft 365 services such as Microsoft Teams, SharePoint Online, OneDrive for Business,

Microsoft Viva, and Microsoft Copilot. He possesses expertise in modern development tools

including SharePoint Framework (SPFx), Teams SDK, Microsoft Graph, Git, TypeScript, React,

Visual Studio, and Azure DevOps.

He actively shares his knowledge and experience through speaking engagements and his blog,

always ready to support and assist the community. Yves served as a reviewer for Microsoft 365

and SharePoint Online Cookbook, by Gaurav Mahajan, Sudeep Ghatak, Nate Chamberlain, and

Scott Brewster.

Rebekka Aalbers has over 15 years of experience in the IT industry. Midway through her ca-

reer, she transitioned to working with Microsoft Partners. Currently, she is a Power Platform

Technical Consultant at Fellowmind, a Microsoft partner active in multiple Northern European

countries. Rebekka specializes in building low-code solutions with the Power Platform, striving

to maximize the platform’s out-of-the-box capabilities and resorting to custom development

only when it adds significant value.

Passionate about helping others embark on their Power Platform journey, Rebekka is an active

member of the technical community. Her contributions were recognized in 2019 when she received

the Microsoft Business Applications MVP award. Known for her fondness of unicorns, she often

incorporates them into her presentations, adding a unique and engaging touch.

Rebekka served as a reviewer for both the first and second editions of Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook

by Eickhel Mendoza. She resides in a rural part of the Netherlands with her husband and two cats.

text:
Preface

Power Apps is a low-code platform for building applications from Microsoft. With this platform,

you can create solutions to your business needs while integrating with other components of the

Power Platform, such as Power Automate and Power BI.

Quite different from the complete online documentation, you will find that this is not your regular

reference book. Instead, this book exposes real-world scenarios and experiences to help you get

a headstart in your Power Apps projects.

By exploring a carefully selected collection of chapters, you will delve into various aspects of Power

Apps. This includes learning the fundamentals of creating canvas apps, designing model-driven

solutions, enhancing apps with custom connectors, and integrating with other platforms. You will

also gain insight into the pro-developer aspects, such as the Power Apps Component Framework

and developing website experiences for external users with Power Pages.

Who this book is for

Since we cover practical use cases, basic knowledge of building applications using Power Apps

is required to take advantage of the solutions explored in this book. You will get a step-by-step

tutorial on building the recipes crafted for each chapter.

What this book covers

Chapter 1, App Maker Basics, serves as the base instructions for building the subsequent recipes.

Instead of repeating these steps in each recipe, we concentrate them in to one chapter for tasks

such as creating a Dataverse solution or building a SharePoint list.

Chapter 2, Building Pixel-Perfect Solutions with Canvas Apps, starts with the best practices for build-

ing canvas apps and continues with creating sample solutions, including coverage of the data

source handling.

filename: Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook_ Build user-friendly apps.pdf
subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Prefacexxiv

Chapter 3, Building from Data with Model-Driven Apps, continues our journey by following a col-

lection of recipes joined together to create an all-around help desk solution. We will also explore

the Entity Relationship Diagram capabilities from the maker Copilot in Power Apps.

Chapter 4, Choosing the Right Data Source for your Applications, will help you to make a sound

decision when determining the data source of your applications. This chapter also explains the

importance of the licensing model on this platform.

Chapter 5, Automating Processes with Power Automate, focuses on several use cases, from inside

and outside the Microsoft ecosystem, to improve business processes using this component of

the Power Platform.

Chapter 6, Extending the Platform, builds upon the concept of enhancing the application-building

process by using components. We will also learn how to extend the platform by creating custom

connectors, using geospatial capabilities, and integrating mixed reality.

Chapter 7, Improving User Experience, looks at how to enrich your user interfaces to make your

applications more appealing to end users. This chapter will also cover how to create a responsive

application using the latest techniques available in Power Apps.

Chapter 8, Power Apps Everywhere, explains all the possible ways to use and integrate Power Apps

on many platforms, from mobile device consumption to embedding scenarios on SharePoint and

Power BI, without forgetting the latest on Microsoft Teams development, including Dataverse

for Teams.

Chapter 9, Empowering Your Applications with AI Builder, focuses on using AI Builder solutions to

improve our applications and processes by bringing artificial intelligence into the mix, including

Copilot.

Chapter 10, Discovering the Power Platform Admin Center, is about learning how to manage the

Power Platform using the tools and settings available in this admin center.

Chapter 11, Tips, Tricks, and Workarounds, offers a collection of hints from the application-building

experience in Power Apps with a set of topics that will help solve or improve a wide variety of

scenarios.

Chapter 12, Advanced Techniques with Power Apps Component Framework, tackles the pro-developer

side by building a Power Apps Component Framework component from scratch. We will look

at setting up our development environment, deploying the component to an environment, and

using it on a canvas app.

nent. It offers a solution to allow external users to interact with our Dataverse data. This chapter

will extend the help desk solution built in previous chapters.

To get the most out of this book

Before diving into building solutions with Power Apps, you are going to need a Microsoft 365

subscription.

You might have one already from your organization, but if you want to have a playground to build

apps, I’m going to give you two suggestions:

• Microsoft 365 Developer Program

This program allows you to have a Microsoft 365 subscription with many features avail-

able: 25 E5 user licenses, apps such as SharePoint, learning resources, and more. It’s the

perfect sandbox environment to create your apps, not only to build Power Apps but also

to learn other technologies from the whole Microsoft 365 ecosystem. This subscription

renews automatically every three months as long as you actively use it.

To get more information, please refer to https://developer.microsoft.com/en-us/

microsoft-365/dev-program.

• Power Apps Developer Plan

This option is ideal if you want a more focused approach to the Power Platform. It offers

a free environment for individual use with the same advantages as a paid plan, including

premium connectors. However, some restrictions exist, such as app sharing and the need

for a Microsoft organizational account.

This subscription has no renewal process; it’s perpetual. For more information, please

visit https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/power-platform/products/power-apps/free.

Power Platform licensing requirements

Power Apps paid plans

The licensing model on this platform depends on the type of connector needed for your data

sources. Standard connectors, such as the one used for SharePoint, don’t require an additional

license besides Microsoft 365, but premium or custom connectors do require a Power Apps license:

• Per app plan

Allows running one app (canvas or model-driven) or portal per user.

• Per user plan

Allows building and using unlimited apps and portals (within service limits).

• Pay-as-you-go plan

Allows a per user plan that charges for the number of apps or portals runs by a user each

month (note that this plan requires an Azure subscription).

To get more insight into the licensing model, please visit https://www.microsoft.com/

en-us/power-platform/products/power-apps/pricing/.

Power Automate paid plans

In Power Automate, three licensing plans allow access to data using premium connectors, custom

connectors, and on-premises data. The difference lies in the capacity of these plans and who will

be the end-user of them:

• There are two user plans: the Power Automate Premium and the Power Automate Hosted

Process. Both let you create unlimited flows, including AI builder service credits, but the

latter adds unattended robotic process automation in a hosted virtual machine.

• On the other hand, the Power Automate Process licenses a bot that runs unattended

robotic process automation.

Using either of these options depends entirely on the analysis of the business process that requires

automation. For detailed information about the pricing of these plans, please refer to https://

www.microsoft.com/en-us/power-platform/products/power-automate/pricing.

App Maker Basics

When comparing technical and culinary cookbooks, you will find certain similarities. Both are

based on recipes that introduce the reader to creating something by following detailed instructions.

For example, in Italian culinary books, there is often a chapter describing how to prepare the

sauce that many recipes will use throughout the book. The same concept applies to this cookbook.

This chapter will explain the basic requirements for the most common scenarios when working

on Power Platform recipes.

The following recipes will serve as a template for specific situations throughout the book:

• How to build a Power Platform solution

• Preparing tables in Dataverse

• Building metadata-enabled storage – SharePoint lists and libraries

• Gathering information with Microsoft Forms

• Setting up a cloud data source – Azure SQL Database

Technical requirements

Depending on the data source you’ll be working with, you might need proper licensing. Start

from the Microsoft 365 Business Basic license for SharePoint through to the Power Apps Premi-

um needed for Dataverse. Please refer to the Preface to get more information about the licensing

requirements.

text:
App Maker Basics2

How to build a Power Platform solution

A Power Platform solution consists of a package that stores all the pieces that compose the solution

you’ve created to solve your business need. It aids in deployment, distribution, and management.

Examples of these pieces can be Power Automate cloud flows, model-driven apps, Power BI re-

ports, or Dataverse tables.

Creating a solution is a straightforward process, but that doesn’t mean you don’t need to follow

specific steps to include best practices for your solutions.

For example, if you need to interact with a particular service, the platform uses a connection

reference. When working with solution components such as cloud flows, the platform will try to

help you by creating connection references for you but using random naming. It becomes even

more complicated if multiple solutions exist within a specific environment. One component from

one solution might use a connection reference from another without you noticing.

Setting up the connection references before creating components can solve these issues easily.

This way, the platform will automatically use the solution’s connection references and the nam-

ing pattern you decide.

Getting ready

After creating the solution, we will need to choose a data source to define the steps required to

configure a connection reference. For this example, we will use SharePoint.

How to do it…

1. Go to the Power Apps maker portal, https://make.powerapps.com, select Solutions from

the left pane, and click + New solution from the toolbar.

2. Before describing the solution, click + New publisher and enter the display name and

name in the Display name and Name fields respectively. Enter a meaningful two-to-

eight-letter Prefix value that will be used for all the elements you will create. Check the

Preview of new object name for an example of how a component will be named. Keep

the default Choice value prefix and click on Save.

3. Back in the New solution pane, enter the desired Display name and Name for the solution,

select your newly created Publisher, and click on Create:

filename: Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook_ Build user-friendly apps.pdf
subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides

Chapter 1 3

Figure 1.1: Solution settings

4. Once the solution is created, from the toolbar, click New | More | Connection Reference.

5. From the panel that opens, set the Display name to AMPI-SharePoint, leave the Name

as it is, and choose SharePoint from the Connector dropdown. If you already have a con-

nection, select it. If not, create one with your credentials by selecting New connection.

6. Repeat Steps 4 and 5 for any other service your solution might require.

How it works…

This creation process will prepare the solution and open it automatically. The SharePoint con-

nection reference will be available to every component that can use it, such as a cloud flow or a

canvas app. This way, we will get a more organized solution for our projects.

Regarding the publishers, from the left pane, click More, Discover all, and then on Publishers

inside the App Management section to see the list of all publishers included in the current en-

vironment.

Preparing tables in Dataverse

Tables are essential to every data source since they represent the backbone of the data structure.

Their designs include column definitions, indexing mechanisms, relationship configurations,

and more.

Getting ready

Building metadata-enabled storage – SharePoint

lists and libraries

SharePoint Online, included in Microsoft 365, provides the perfect platform for secure content

management, collaboration, and communication through dedicated sites.

This platform is commonly used as a data source for Power Apps solutions since it provides Mic-

not comparable to a full-fledged relational database, but it’s simple to use and comes included

Gathering information with Microsoft Forms

Web forms are an excellent tool for gathering information. Whether you require feedback from

a specific process, an event registration, or even a simple contact form, you must clearly define

Microsoft Forms gives you an easy way to create them with an easy-to-use interface that allows

information from external users to your organization, as we will discover in Chapter 9, Empow-

from our customers.

Microsoft Forms is a service that goes beyond Microsoft 365. You can even use it with your per-

sonal Microsoft accounts. However, you must create the forms inside your tenant to use it with

Power Platform. For this recipe, we will learn the necessary steps to build a form.

Setting up a cloud data source – Azure SQL

Database

Azure SQL is a suite of SQL database services on the Azure cloud. It offers automated backups,

high availability, and advanced security, making it ideal for traditional SQL database needs with

cloud scalability and integration.

While Azure SQL provides extensive control for database management, Dataverse offers a higher

level of abstraction for faster and easier development. Depending on the needs of your project,

sometimes having granular control of your database is a must.

This recipe will help you build an Azure SQL database that might be needed for an app.

Getting ready

To start working with Azure SQL databases, you will need an Azure subscription. You can request

a free version with credit for 30 days to test all the services available on this cloud platform. Apply

for it at https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/free.

How to do it…

1. Go to the Azure portal at https://portal.azure.com and click Create a resource. This

action will take you to Azure Marketplace. Using the search field, enter SQL Database

and hit Enter.

2. From the list of services, select SQL Database and then click Create. This action will open

the Create SQL Database page, as seen in the following screenshot:

Enter the database name in the Database name field and select a server.

times. Leave the default Use Microsoft Entra-only authentication as the Authentication

Building Pixel-Perfect Solutions

with Canvas Apps

Power Apps is the platform of choice for building business solutions using a low-code method.

The platform is suitable for individuals within an organization eager to learn about the technology

while bringing their business process expertise to the table.

Power Apps’ canvas apps allow you to create pixel-perfect implementations of user interfaces. As

the name suggests, they offer various tools to build any imaginable design in your applications,

allowing you to design and develop apps of any type, whether it is a critical business system or

a simple tracking application.

During this chapter, we will discover how to create a set of applications that will give you an

insight into the different approaches to building canvas apps. We will also learn how to set up

various data sources for our applications.

This chapter consists of the following recipes:

• Discovering best practices when building canvas apps

• Creating an incident tracking solution – setting up the data source

• Creating an incident tracking solution – building the user interface

• Improving SharePoint list forms with the help of Power Apps

• Creating a canvas app from existing data

Building Pixel-Perfect Solutions with Canvas Apps18

Discovering best practices when building canvas

apps

Setting up data sources, defining business process flows, and creating user interfaces – all these

tasks are pieces of an application-building process. These pieces come together to accomplish

one main goal: to build a solution that solves a specific need.

One of the things you need to consider is the maintainability of your app. Whether fixing bugs

or adding new features, using best practices is always a good idea. No matter your technology,

well-documented code is easier to maintain.

Even though Power Apps is a low-code platform, you must consider certain things before building

applications. Like any other developer team, you need to establish code standards. These stan-

dards allow your team to be more productive by setting predefined patterns for variable naming,

control usage, and coding methodology.

Variable naming

Proper naming gives your developers instant insight into the scope of your variables. For example,

if a variable name prefix starts with lcl (short for local), it means its value will only be available

on the current screen. On the other hand, using gbl (short for global) means that this variable

is accessible across the whole application.

These examples might seem trivial, but if another developer needs to maintain your app or your

app serves as a template for other apps in your organization, setting these patterns from the start

can help the application-building process and maintainability.

Control usage

One key point of an application’s success is performance. If an application starts slowly or takes

several seconds to perform a task, it hurts user adoption.

Here are a couple of examples of this:

• A great-looking app that uses many controls to build its user interface but hurts perfor-

mance each time the screens are rendered.

• Displaying data to a user using a gallery inside a gallery. This approach might be tempting

to present master-detail data, but this would be a significant slowdown in your application.

To avoid this, you need to learn the performance points of your platform. In Power Apps, one of

the main recommendations for improving responsiveness is to reduce the number of controls.

Coding methodology

This concept describes a set of rules to regulate the development process in a low-code team.

Your solution infrastructure can also help you make an informed decision on how to build your

application:

• If you have data that rarely changes, you can create collections to avoid round-trips each

time data is needed. Even more, if you have data that never changes, you can import this

as static data inside your app for speedier access. Refer to Chapter 4, Choosing the Right

Data Source for Your Applications, for a recipe example on this.

• Taking advantage of the features available in your data source can significantly improve

your application performance. For example, when using Dataverse or any other relation-

al database, there is a significant difference when querying data if you use data source

views instead of building the actual query in your application logic, especially if it needs

complex relationships. Using these views gives you cleaner code while also enhancing

performance. This improvement relies on the fact that the data source engine is the one

executing the data processing instead of the application itself.

3

Building from Data with Model-

Driven Apps

Model-driven apps are the data-centric siblings of canvas apps. They get their foundation from

the business data model, taking the approach of placing building blocks on top of data. These

blocks spread in a standard responsive layout, which allows the creation of a solution that adapts

to any device.

Even though analyzing and setting up the data source is one of the main objectives of any ap-

plication, this is the primary objective in model-driven apps. A complete understanding of the

business process allows you to design your data model with a solid structure to support the

proposed solution. The last step would be to build the app on top of this model.

Licensing requirements

When building model-driven solutions, there are some specific licensing requirements. Please

refer to the Preface section of this book to get more information about the licensing model of this

platform.

Exploring Dataverse

When we talk about the data model for model-driven apps, we mean Dataverse. The data gets

stored in tables just like traditional databases. The difference is the rich set of business-oriented

features:

• Use an out-of-the-box set of standard business tables with the ability to add your custom

tables

• Create a table, and the platform will automatically add all columns to address the under-

lying process requirements, such as owner info, tracking, status, versioning, and the like

• Structure your data with various column data types, which helps in complex data mod-

eling scenarios

• Design relationships and define keys for standard and custom tables to ensure data in-

tegrity across the service

• Enforce security on roles, records, and column levels, giving you complete flexibility when

setting up data access

• Add business features right from the table configuration: data consumption through views,

data manipulation through forms, data visualization through dashboards and charts, and

last but not least, business rules to apply a set of validations and logic without writing code

Chapter 3 41

Here’s an example of what tables look like:

Figure 3.1: Table example in Dataverse

To store these tables, Dataverse uses environments. Environments serve as a container for data

and all the components that interact with it, such as applications, cloud flows, and business

processes.

Inside these environments, Dataverse manages solutions to package apps and components that

serve a specific purpose. This feature allows the transfer of these packages between environ-

ments and, thus, the implementation of application lifecycle management (ALM) for the whole

platform. For more information, please refer to https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/power-

platform/alm/basics-alm.

Dataverse is also the service that most Dynamics 365 applications use to store their data – this

means that you can interact with the data that your business is already using.

Configuring your environment

Configuring a Dataverse database for the first time will create a set of business-centric tables, such

as Accounts and Contacts. Starting from these, you can add the custom tables your processes

might need to achieve their goal. In this recipe, we will start creating the building blocks of an

application to handle a Helpdesk service.

Getting ready

To build our solution, we will start by setting up a new environment that will act as our develop-

ment area. Then, we can pack our solution and deploy it wherever it is needed.

Building the model-driven app

Creating a low-code application entails a different methodology for the application-building

process. When using other technologies, you might need to choose the language, infrastructure,

database system, and more. For model-driven applications, the essential principle is to create

everything from the data structure and then build the components from there.

Getting ready

Per our example, the Helpdesk solution will package all elements required for our application,

such as tables, dashboards, and so on. You can export all components in just one package and

then import them into the destination environment.

We will use the Modern app designer to build the application. This designer allows more rapid

application development, although it doesn’t have the complete list of features that the classic

designer has. However, there is always a Switch to classic button to fall back to the classic de-

signer when needed.

Setting up business process logic

Every business process has a step-by-step procedure that defines every requirement, objective,

and resolution from start to end. Companies build on and improve these procedures depending

on the business needs and even create departments to work exclusively on this.

Getting ready

Model-driven apps help set up these rules by providing several tools to define business logic at

various platform levels. You can incorporate data validation rules, structured data flows to guide

the end user, and even trigger workflows for specific events in your processes. These are just some

examples of what you can achieve with this platform.

• Guiding ticket processing by ensuring the user inputs the required information in each

defined step with the help of a business process flow (BPF). This component also allows

Designing dashboards to visualize data

When working with business processes that deal with data, one of the main goals for organiza-

opportunity is vital, so having an easy way to interact with data is very important.

Dashboards are a feature in Dataverse that allows you to display a mix of graphs, grids of data,

and web resources in one place. For example, web resources can include iframe objects, which

can display content from another website inside a model-driven application.

Building on the example used throughout this chapter, let’s add more value to the Helpdesk

Integrating canvas apps inside model-driven apps

One of the best features of canvas apps is the ability to access multiple connectors from the same

app. We can use this strength by embedding a canvas app as a component.

These are some scenarios in which this can be very helpful:

• A canvas application that is already in use by the organization, and we want to integrate

it into our model-driven solution.

• A canvas app that connects to a legacy system using the on-premises data gateway.

• An employee tracking system that gives us information about which of our customer

locations our support staff is working at any given moment. This data could be helpful

to see whether we already have someone from support at the customer’s location when

a new ticket arrives.

Now, let’s see how to integrate a canvas app into our model-driven solution.

How to do it…

form of the Main type.

Power Apps is still evolving regarding the form designer experience, so we

still need to use the classic version to add some components.

Deploying your solution to your production

environment

Whether building a full-fledged model-driven or canvas application, you should consider building

solutions with an ALM insight. This concept allows you to differentiate between a development,

testing, and production environment, their role in your application-building process, and how

your solution will get deployed through them. These environment types are just an example of

an ALM implementation. You can discover more information about ALM in Power Platform here:

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-platform/alm/basics-alm.

Power Platform leverages the concept of pipelines as the tool to connect environments and then

deploy solutions between them. They can be as straightforward or complex as you or your orga-

nization want them to be. To get more information, follow this link: https://learn.microsoft.

com/en-us/power-platform/alm/pipelines.

Getting ready

To fully integrate ALM into your solutions, you should keep in mind that it’s only available for

environments with a Dataverse database. That’s one of the selling points of this critical element

of Power Platform: it maintains your data and helps you manage the solutions you create to

handle this data.

To build this recipe, we will need to have at least another environment to deploy the solution. Please

refer to the first recipe of this chapter, Configuring the environment, to create a new environment.

How to do it…

1. Open your solution from the Power Apps maker portal.

2. On the left pane, you will find a rocket icon. This icon refers to the pipeline we will use

to deploy our solution to another environment. Click on it to open this section. The first

time you open the pipelines, it will take a while to set up everything for you.

Discovering the Copilot experience when building

model-driven apps

So far, we have followed the complete process of building a solution using Power Platform. From

creating the environment to the deployment process of our Helpdesk application. Every step of

this process follows a specific purpose, allowing a team of makers to focus on particular tasks. One

can be in charge of the data model, another can build the app, and another can create a custom

page to extend capabilities. In this era of artificial intelligence assistance in every platform, why

not assign one of these tasks to the Power Platform Copilot?

You will discover that Copilot is present in certain parts of the application-building process. We

can find it when building canvas apps, dealing with Power Fx code, and creating the data model.

Soon, it will play a more significant role in various aspects of Power Platform. To keep track of all

the improvements, follow this link: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-platform/

copilot.

Getting ready

We will take advantage of the data model capabilities of Copilot in Power Apps to prepare some

of the tables mentioned in this chapter, but only for creating the new tables since Copilot is still

learning how to deal with existing tables from an actual prompt. From there, we could continue

building the app as we did through this chapter.

We will recreate the Defining data structures recipe with the help of Copilot. Once the environ-

ment and solution are ready by following the first two recipes, we will land in the data structure

creation process. Using an AI prompt, we will create the following tables: Project, Ticket, and

Ticket operation.

Copilot doesn’t have a parameter to define the solution it will be working on. As a workaround,

we will adapt the maker portal to have the Helpdesk solution as default for new objects in the

environment. This way, everything done by Copilot will be included in our solution.

4

Choosing the Right Data Source

for Your Applications

Selecting the right data source is one of the most important decisions when designing your ap-

plication infrastructure. Many factors come into play, such as features, security, speed, pricing,

and integrations.

Thankfully, your solution’s needs will help you select the right one. For example, it’s better to use

a database with a certified connector rather than building it yourself; if your application needs

to store a specific data type, it’s best to choose a database that can handle it natively. Another

example is when working with canvas apps: setting up different data sources on the same appli-

cation opens many possibilities when interacting with data.

Before diving into this chapter, we will go into more detail about Power Platform’s licensing

model, a crucial topic for Power Platform makers. Having covered this concept, we will be able

to discuss data in the Power Platform with the help of these recipes:

• Reducing your application complexity by using Azure SQL database views

• Choosing the right data source – real-world tests

• Integrating on-premises data with canvas apps

• Improving application speed and responsiveness by using static data

• Consuming external data by using dataflows

subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Choosing the Right Data Source for Your Applications82

Technical requirements

To thoroughly test all the recipes tackling various forms of data sources, we will need a Power

Apps or Power Automate licensing plan. Please refer to the Preface to get more information about

the licensing requirements.

Visit our GitHub repository for the code samples of this chapter: https://github.com/

PacktPublishing/Microsoft-Power-Apps-Cookbook-Third-Edition/tree/main/Chapter-04.

Data sources and the licensing model

We need to understand the unique differentiator that makes us need a license: whether a con-

nector is labeled premium. This tag activates the end-user license requirement when using the

app you created, even if you own a license to build it.

The current licensing model for end users is reminiscent of the SQL Server Client Access Licens-

es (CALs), in which every user accessing the server requires a pass. It is the same for the Power

Platform. You add capacity to your environments to allow unlicensed users to access your app.

The platform recognizes which apps are built with premium connectors to access data or services.

When you access the details of your apps or flows, you will see a License designation or Plan

that will inform you about this:

text:
Choosing the Right Data Source for Your Applications84

When designing your infrastructure, always consider the licensing model beforehand to avoid

surprises at the end of your project when the user base starts growing.

However, you need to be conscious of the value of this consumption model. Previously, you would

need to buy licenses for every user using your app at any moment instead of purchasing passes

only for the actual users. Let me explain this with an example.

Let’s pretend we have an organization with 10 employees that would use your app at some spe-

cific points in time:

• Five administrative employees will use the app daily

• Four managers will use the app quarterly

• One employee from marketing will use the app occasionally

In the previous model, if the license price were 10 USD, you would have had to pay 100 USD per

month. With the consumption model, you can make calculations based on usage to allow a cer-

tain amount of simultaneous users, say six, which would reduce the price to 60 USD per month.

Keep in mind that the Power Apps per-app licenses used for the consumption model can only be

acquired through Microsoft Partners. Please refer to this link to get the current Power Apps pricing

plans: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/power-platform/products/power-apps/pricing.

Power Apps/Power Automate for Microsoft 365

You don’t always need a license to work with Power Apps or Power Automate. Starting from the

regular Microsoft 365 Business Basic license, you can build apps in the context of Microsoft 365

using standard connectors.

Real-world applications use SharePoint as their data source without incurring extra costs, even for

mobile apps with offline capabilities. To get more information regarding this topic, visit https://

learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-platform/admin/pricing-billing-skus#power-apps-

and-power-automate-for-microsoft-365.

Furthermore, Dataverse for Teams allows us to build apps with a light version of Dataverse in

the Microsoft Teams platform, using the same license required to use Teams. Refer to Chapter 8,

Power Apps Everywhere, for recipe examples.

Let’s deep dive into the data source recipes with a clear concept of the licensing model in mind.

Chapter 4 85

Choosing the right data source – real-world tests

Every data source has unique features that make it ideal for specific scenarios, whether you need

a robust relational database, a document-centric infrastructure, or a lightweight approach for

mobile applications.

This recipe will test some of Microsoft’s most well-known players in the data source world: Dat-

averse, SharePoint, and Azure SQL Database. With the help of Power Automate, we will test

both the reading and writing speeds of these three contestants.

Getting ready

The first requirement is to have the same data structure for each service:

• A list with the default Title column in SharePoint

• A table with a Title field in Azure SQL using the Basic performance tier

• A table with a Title column in Dataverse

Refer to Chapter 1, App Maker Basics, for instructions on creating these data sources. Once complete,

proceed to the Power Automate portal to build our tests at https://make.powerautomate.com/.

At the time of writing, Power Automate is transitioning to a new designer based on the one used

in Azure Logic Apps, the so-called father of Power Automate. This new designer includes excellent

features to help makers build their cloud flows faster and more reliably. An example is the ability

to save cloud flows as drafts, even with errors.

For the sake of having the most up-to-date version, we will use the new designer throughout

the book. However, when creating cloud flows from solutions, we land on the now-called Classic

designer. To use the new designer, save the flow and open it again.

How to do it…

1. We will need some data to run our test, so let’s build a Power Automate cloud flow to write

data into SharePoint. First, go to Solutions and create a new solution named Speed tests.

Another workaround is to enable Create new canvas apps and cloud flows in Dat-

averse solutions in your environment from the Power Platform admin center and

then set your working solution as the preferred one. For more information on these

topics, please visit https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-apps/maker/

canvas-apps/add-app-solution-default and https://learn.microsoft.com/

en-us/power-apps/maker/data-platform/preferred-solution.

subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides

2. First, let’s prepare our solutions’ connection references so we can name them appropriately.

From the toolbar, click New | More | Connection Reference. From the open panel, set the

Display name to SpeedTest-SharePoint, leave the Name as it is, and choose SharePoint

from the Connector dropdown. If you already have a connection, select it. If not, create

From the open panel, set the Display name to SpeedTest-SharePoint-Site, choose Data

Select the previously created Site environment variable from the Site dropdown, and

Configure it to use your SharePoint site and list environment variables by selecting Enter

Connectors retrieve data in small portions (by default, 100 items), which

serves as a protective measure to prevent accidentally querying large

amounts of data. Consider a scenario when querying a massive database

without applying the correct filters; the platform would have to handle a

significant amount of work.

For specific scenarios where you need to read more than the default, we can

use pagination. This concept translates into getting a predefined amount of

data in chunks. To get more information about this, please visit https://

learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-automate/dataverse/list-

rows?tabs=edit-with-copilot#turn-on-pagination-to-request-

more-than-5000-rows

How it works…

The six cloud flows we have just created will help you get an overview of these data sources’ da-

ta-handling speeds. You will need to execute the insert cloud flows to have data for our reading

tests. In my test scenarios, these were the execution times I obtained on an average of three runs:

Test SharePoint Azure SQL Dataverse

Writing test 04:08 minutes 04:14 minutes 04:24 minutes

subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Choosing the Right Data Source for Your Applications90

If we look at the reading test, we get a surprising result on an average of three runs:

Test SharePoint Azure SQL Dataverse

Reading test 5 seconds 347 ms 2 seconds

Table 4.2: Read results

We got 500 records really fast. This kind of outcome is mainly due to the caching mechanisms

that all three have in their infrastructure. When returning data, it also depends on each specific

platform: SharePoint and Dataverse return metadata with each query, but Azure SQL does not. If

we improve the requests by specifying only the fields we need, we will get faster response times.

For example, querying only the Title column in Dataverse lowered the results to approximately

320 milliseconds.

However, this opens a whole new debate. If the data in our application is mainly for reading

purposes, then why not use SharePoint? It is cheaper and, while not the quickest, still performed

well in the reading test; this, of course, will depend on the complexity of your entities. Using only

one field is not the same as including complex data types in the mix. Still, this specific SharePoint

result is something to bear in mind.

There’s more…

The platform used for SharePoint and Dataverse has predefined performance limits to comply

with SLAs and response times. For the Azure SQL test, the database was running on the Basic tier

level. Increasing the tier level improves performance on memory or throughput levels. You can

even upgrade the database to a more robust and performant level. Consider these skills when

deciding on your data sources.

I hope this workshop sparks your curiosity regarding the complexity behind the data sources you

will use in your developments.

SharePoint Online performance considerations

When working with SharePoint Online, you need to remember that you are working with a web

application with specific response and performance levels to provide the best user experience.

Microsoft has designed a set of rules to meet this, for example, setting a view threshold of 5,000

elements per list. Even though a list can hold up to 30 million items, querying data exceeding

this threshold limit will result in platform errors, making the list unresponsive.

filename: Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook_ Build user-friendly apps.pdf
subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Chapter 4 91

These are a few recommendations to keep your lists performant:

• Set an index for the columns you wish to filter. Remember to do this beforehand since

you cannot change it if you have exceeded the threshold.

• Prepare segmented views for lists that might carry a large number of items. Examples can

be categories, years, and departments.

• To avoid performance issues, build views with fewer than 12 People, Lookup, or Managed

metadata columns.

For reference on this subject, check out the following links:

• https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/manage-large-lists-and-

libraries-in-sharepoint-b8588dae-9387-48c2-9248-c24122f07c59

• https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/use-filtering-to-modify-a-

sharepoint-view-3d8efc52-0808-4731-8f9b-3dfaeacea3d4

Reducing your application complexity by using

Azure SQL database views

Performance is one of the main objectives of almost all data source engines. Database developers

tweak the innards of their core systems to make them as efficient as possible while also adding

new features for app makers. Knowing this, why not leverage the efficiency of these platforms?

That’s the primary purpose of this recipe: to learn how to improve our apps’ responsiveness and

complexity by making the data sources work for us.

Getting ready

To build our use case, we will improve an application connected to an Azure SQL database. The

database needs five tables that will make up our data catalog. The scripts to create them and the

base apps are available in the GitHub repository mentioned in the Technical requirements section.

If you don’t have an Azure subscription, you can request a free version with credit for 30 days to

test all the services available on this cloud platform. Apply for it at https://azure.microsoft.

com/en-us/free/.

How to do it…

Please refer to Chapter 1, App Maker Basics, for steps that will help you build the Azure SQL data-

base needed for the app. First, download all the files from the repository and have them ready.

can use either the Azure Data Studio, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure-data-

studio/download-azure-data-studio, or the Azure portal itself. Accessing it through the

the Open query option in the toolbar and execute them one by one by clicking Run on the

toolbar. In the following figure, you can see how to access the Query editor:

If you can’t get the data from your database, remove all the tables already connected to

the application and add them again.

8. Let’s inspect the gallery’s Items property:

Filter(

AddColumns(

tickets,

Technician,

LookUp(

technicians,

id = technician_id, full_name

),

Status,

LookUp(

ticket_status,

id = status_id,

description

),

Priority,

LookUp(

ticket_priority,

id = priority_id,

description

)

),

)

As you can see, several complex formulas accomplish the relationships between the five

tables. First, we filter the tickets for the selected customer, and then we add columns to

get the technician’s name and the descriptions for the statuses and priorities.

Having this many formulas to query data reduces performance because we make multiple

calls to the backend to get the data. It also adds a maintenance overhead for your app.

Let’s improve this by using an Azure SQL view.

9. Connect to your Azure SQL database using your preferred method and execute the pro-

vided script, VIEW – TicketData.sql

subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Chapter 4 95

10. To include the vw_TicketData view in the app, click on the Data panel on the left (repre-

sented by a database icon), click Add data, search for SQL, and pick SQL Server. Select your

previously configured connection, choose the vw_TicketData view from your database,

and click Connect when you’re finished.

Using this database view, we can accomplish several tasks:

• Reduce the complexity of the gallery’s Items property by removing all the formulas,

leaving just the filter for the selected customer:

Filter(

vw_TicketData,

customer_id = CustomersCbx.Selected.id

)

• Eliminate the need for the lookup tables, as they don’t need to be connected to

our app to get the descriptions of the statuses, priorities, or technician data. You

can even remove the tickets table because the view provides all the information

needed, leaving you just with customers and vw_TicketData in the Data panel

of your app.

How it works…

The application performance improves because the relationship process is executed at the data-

base level and not from the Power Apps app. We also decreased the data transfers between the

data source and our app when we reduced the tables connected to the app. The code also looks

cleaner, and it’s easier to maintain.

The script to create the view links the database tables using the built-in SQL language. It gets

only the fields we need and joins the four tables by their identity fields.

This approach also adds another enhancement regarding development workload: the team in

charge of database maintenance and performance can provide us with these views because they

have better insights on the best way to obtain this data.

There’s more…

This recipe is just an example of how the capabilities of our chosen data source can improve

our app. It will be helpful if you know the features available in your data service so you can take

advantage of them when building your apps.

filename: Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook_ Build user-friendly apps.pdf
subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Choosing the Right Data Source for Your Applications96

Another similar example is the use of Dataverse table views. It works on the same principles as

the SQL database views, giving us just the columns we need with the required data. We can then

use these views in our apps by invoking them in our Filter clause:

Filter(Tickets, 'Tickets (Views)'.'Active Tickets')

The list doesn’t stop here; you can use store procedures to build code into your SQL database, apply

business rules to your Dataverse tables, improve user authentication, and more. These are just

examples of the capabilities available for these two data sources. Make your application-building

process more straightforward by leveraging them.

Integrating on-premises data with canvas apps

Not all data lives in the cloud; sometimes, organizational restrictions, legacy platforms that are too

expensive to migrate, or complex network infrastructures make our job a little more complicated.

There are different ways to overcome these challenges, such as synchronization processes and

exposing application interfaces outside the local infrastructure. Thankfully, one of the most

significant features of the Power Platform is the ability to connect to on-premises services using

a data gateway.

The on-premises data gateway acts as a bridge between the local services and Azure. There is

no need to set authentication methods for the services you need to access; this only allows the

platforms to be visible to each other—authentication takes place afterward.

Gateways not only allow you to connect to databases; they also include access to the file system,

local SharePoint servers, and other on-premises services.

Getting ready

Once you have identified the on-premises system you want to access, you need to choose the type

of gateway you want to use: regular or personal mode. As the names imply, the difference lies in

the number of users. The personal mode only allows one user, and the other shares the gateway

between multiple users.

There are specific use cases for each. For example, why configure a gateway for the entire orga-

nization if only the data analyst needs to gather information from the local SQL server? She can

install the personal gateway on her computer to collect data.

text:
Chapter 4 101

Improving application speed and responsiveness by

using static data

When working with cloud data, there are situations where the data collection process can be

slow. Many factors can add delays when obtaining data: network speed, signal strength, and

data source infrastructure, to name a few.

That’s why you need to consider the data you are working with. Where is it located? What is its

availability? How changeable is it?

In this recipe, we will try to add a solution to the last question. If data doesn’t change, why not

make it static? We are not talking about adding the data in the actual code; we will add the data

as a resource for the application, just like when adding an image.

Getting ready

As an example of data that rarely changes, we have provided a list of countries in an Excel

file, countries.xlsx, in this chapter’s repository: https://github.com/PacktPublishing/

Microsoft-Power-Apps-Cookbook-Third-Edition/tree/main/Chapter-04.

How to do it…

1. Go to the Power Apps maker portal and create a new canvas app; select either phone or

tablet layout. From the left pane, select Data, click on Add data, search for Import from

Excel, and choose this connection.

2. This action will prompt you to select an Excel file from your file system; pick the provided

one or any other from your computer, given that the data on this file has a table defined.

For more information on this requirement, visit https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/

office/overview-of-excel-tables-7ab0bb7d-3a9e-4b56-a3c9-6c94334e492c.

3. Once the file finishes uploading, the right pane will display a list of tables inside the file

for you to select. Choose one and click Connect. The selected Excel table will appear on

the list of data sources as if it were a connected one.

How it works…

If your data rarely changes, you can add it as a resource in your application. Keep in mind, though,

that the amount of data will increase the size of your app. A 3 MB Excel file is no candidate for this.

Think of these resources as you would think about images. The smaller the file size, the better.

filename: Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook_ Build user-friendly apps.pdf
subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Choosing the Right Data Source for Your Applications102

With the provided file, you can build an app that can help you search for a list of countries:

Figure 4.12: List of static countries’ data

Now, you can check your apps for static data candidates and improve their performance by re-

ducing data sources’ connections.

There’s more…

There’s another approach to static data, this time with custom pages. This type of Power App

includes the capacity to import web resources (.resx) commonly used for model-driven apps.

In this case, we can use these resource files to add localization for our applications. To get more

information, visit https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-apps/maker/model-driven-

apps/custom-page-localize

Consuming external data by using Dataflows

The data for your solutions can come from various sources, such as relational databases, on-prem-

ises data, analytics data, APIs, and even regular files. These sources can be located anywhere and

may not have the infrastructure to provide data.

Chapter 4 103

Dataflows aim to be an instrument for gathering all kinds of data sources. With this tool, you

can consolidate all the required data, related or not, into Dataverse, where you can improve the

collected information by adding views, relationships, and the like. Dataflows not only gather

data but also allow you to transform it while doing it.

Power Query, the same technology used in Power BI, helps with these transformations, giving you a

complete set of features to shape your data. For more information about Power Query, please refer

to https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-query/power-query-what-is-power-query.

Dataflows can run manually or on a schedule. They live in your environments, so you can have

them running in your test environment, gathering data from test sources, and have different

ones in production.

For this recipe, we will use a different approach other than connecting to a database. Thanks to the

AccuWeather developer API, we will get weather data and save the forecast into a Dataverse table.

Getting ready

According to the current documentation, you should need a license to use Dataflows because it is

not part of the features included in a Developer plan. However, you can create and use Dataflows

anyway. This is something that needs clarification from Microsoft’s documentation and has been

reported to them already.

The next thing we will need to do is register for a free developer account with AccuWeather at

https://developer .accuweather.com. After registering, go to MY APPS and create an app with

an API key to access their system. The limited trial is a free service that allows 50 calls daily and

just one key per developer, but it suits our objective well. Make sure you select Core Weather

Limited Trial under Products when creating the app.

How to do it…

1. Go to the Power Apps maker portal to create a solution for this recipe. From this solution,

click on New | Automation | Dataflow. In the open dialog, name it, for example, Weather

data, and click Create.

There’s more…

Dataflows are an excellent tool for ingesting data from different sources without the need to build

an infrastructure to gather or transform the data. However, there are some limitations that you

might need to consider, which you can learn about here: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/

power-bi/transform-model/dataflows/dataflows-features-limitations.

A helpful feature of dataflows is that they also serve as synchronization tools. When defining

the load data settings, there is an option called Delete rows that no longer exist in the query

output. This change requires the alternate key field to be mandatory as it uses it for comparison

purposes when loading new data:

Figure 4.19: Dataflow load settings for sync

This setting, tied to a scheduled refresh, turns dataflows effectively into a sync mechanism. In our

tests, we loaded data from an Azure SQL database into a technicians table with these columns: ID,

Full name, Email, and Location. After the first load, we deleted a record from the SQL database,

and on the next refresh, the deleted record was removed on Dataverse.

One more concept that we need to consider is that you can configure a dataflow to load several

tables simultaneously. As the previous figure shows, we are loading both SalesLT Products and

technicians on the same dataflow.

As you can see, this is an excellent tool for integrating external data into Dataverse. Once there,

you can have complete control over security, automatization, and data consumption.

5

Automating Processes with

Power Automate

Power Platform provides different solutions to solve business organizations’ needs: Power BI to

analyze data, Power Apps to build applications, Power Pages to build customer-facing websites

and portals, Copilot Studio to interact with users, and Power Automate to automate processes

effectively.

In this chapter, we will discuss Power Automate, which aims to improve business processes

with a series of actions to help streamline existing operations. Examples of these actions include

executing procedures based on specific events, building data integration systems, automating

repetitive tasks, and more.

Before diving into this chapter, we will also cover a key topic regarding the different types of flows.

Having understood this concept, we can then build recipes using examples for diverse scenarios:

• Creating a sales survey solution with Microsoft Forms

• Building a file-processing automation for SharePoint libraries

• Overcoming Power Apps delegation with Power Automate

• Creating a modular solution with Power Automate

• Automating legacy applications using desktop flows

• Integrating Google Forms with Dataverse using cloud flows

filename: Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook_ Build user-friendly apps.pdf
subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Automating Processes with Power Automate112

Technical requirements

There might be a license requirement depending on the services you need to connect to Power

Automate. Please refer to the Preface section of this book for more information.

At the time of writing, Power Automate does not use the new designer when creating a flow from

a solution. The workaround is to create it, save it, and then open it again.

If you see the classic designer, add a New step, search for Compose, and enter any text as the

Inputs. We are doing this workaround to be able to save the cloud flow, close it, and then open it

again to get the new flow designer. You can delete the Compose action afterward.

This chapter will follow the new designer’s steps to provide the most up-to-date instructions.

The code for this chapter’s recipes is available from our GitHub repository at https://github.com/

PacktPublishing/Microsoft-Power-Apps-Cookbook-Third-Edition/tree/main/Chapter-05.

The different types of flows

Power Automate offers five types of flows to provide organizations with as many options as pos-

sible. Each of these types aims to solve specific scenarios.

Automated cloud flow

These cloud flows are executed when a specific action triggers them – for example:

• When a new email arrives in Gmail

• When a new file gets uploaded to SharePoint

You can build solutions around them, such as the following:

• When a new email has the word “invoice” in the title, extract the attachments and copy

them to the Finance SharePoint document library.

• When a new tweet gets posted, send the content to AI Builder for sentiment analysis,

and then send a Microsoft Teams notification to the marketing department if the result

is negative.

Instant cloud flow

If you need to trigger a cloud flow manually, an instant cloud flow is the option you want. The

following are examples of this kind of situation:

• Clicking a button on your mobile phone

filename: Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook_ Build user-friendly apps.pdf
subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Chapter 5 113

• Executing flows from a canvas app

• Selecting a file in a SharePoint document library

These cloud flows can trigger solutions such as:

• Creating an on-demand report from the current sales records

• Notifying a user through Microsoft Teams from a canvas app

• Requesting a signature for a selected file in SharePoint

Scheduled cloud flow

As the name implies, these cloud flows are executed at a specific date and time and with a defined

recurrence. These are some of the possible use cases:

• Performing a monthly backup of a particular folder to your personal OneDrive

• Creating and sending timesheet reports every two weeks

• Performing a daily cleanup of an Azure SQL table

Business process flow

As mentioned in Chapter 3, Building from Data with Model-Driven Apps, these flows act as a guiding

system for Dataverse tables to help users through the data-gathering process. Examples include

the following:

• Turning leads into opportunities for the sales department

• Managing a support case in a help desk system

Desktop flow

These desktop flows bring Robotic Process Automation (RPA) to Power Automate by allowing

you to record your interaction with web and desktop applications, which avoids repetitive tasks

by automating the playback of these interactions. Using these can help in the following cases:

• Data entry on a legacy ERP system that has no API to interact with

• Recording the customization process of a particular application to replicate it on different

devices

As you can see, there is a diversity of flows aimed at solving almost every business requirement,

and it doesn’t stop there; the platform keeps evolving to offer even more features to help you

achieve your goals. The following recipes will help you get a taste of all the possibilities that

Power Automate offers.

Creating a sales survey solution with Microsoft Forms

Web forms are an excellent tool for gathering information. Whether you require feedback from

a specific process, an event registration, or even a simple contact form, you must clearly define

the fields to collect the data in these forms.

Microsoft Forms gives you an easy way to create them with an easy-to-use interface that allows

you to quickly create forms, quizzes, and polls. We will use this service to complete our solution

by integrating an automated cloud flow using Power Automate.

The first step is to design a sales survey, and then, depending on the answers received, we will

notify a team to further engage with the customer.

The way we notify people in our organizations has evolved since emails. The norm is using email

for external users and collaboration tools for internal ones. Users prefer receiving rich notifications

with which they can interact directly using their platform of choice.

Adaptive Cards help improve notifications by applying user interface elements, which act and

look native in the platform where they are delivered.

The following is an example of an Adaptive Card:

laboration tools, such as Microsoft Teams. To get more information, please refer to https://

adaptivecards.io.

Getting ready

To recreate this recipe, you will need a regular Microsoft 365 Business plan (Microsoft 365 Business

Basic and up) or a Microsoft personal account (Outlook, Hotmail, or Microsoft). Both account

For this recipe, we will prepare a solution containing an automated cloud flow that will automate

the responses from a sales survey, created using Microsoft Forms. Follow the instructions found

for the form:

How to do it…

1. Head to Microsoft Forms to build the required form. Once ready, we can start building

actions that will get triggered when we start receiving the responses.

2. Go to the Power Automate portal, https://make.powerautomate.com, and create a solu-

tion to hold the cloud flow.

Another option for sending rich notifications, available exclusively for Microsoft Teams, is Cards

Building a file processing automation for SharePoint

libraries

Improving business activities, especially recurring ones, is a top priority in every organization.

Repeating a set of actions for a business process can be prone to errors because the personnel

tends to replicate actions without validation. Power Automate builds upon this need to help

organizations automate their tasks so that people can focus on the business.

In this recipe, we will automate a business process using a SharePoint document library that

handles the quotes of a given company. Microsoft Word will generate these quotes with defined

metadata to help classify their contents.

Users can manually execute a cloud flow when a quote is complete, converting the document

into a PDF file with the same metadata as the original one. It also notifies the Finance team if

the quote is over $100,000.

Getting ready

When using SharePoint, as far as licensing goes, a regular Microsoft 365 Business Basic license

is required to include this service in your organization. We won’t need an additional license, as

we will use standard connectors on the Power Automate side. Regarding the document library,

please refer to Chapter 1, App Maker Basics, for instructions on how to create it.

text:
Chapter 5 121

How to do it…

1. First, let’s start by building the document library. For this recipe, name it Quotes and add

the following columns:

Column type Name Extra

Text Quote

Choice Department Choices: Finance, HR, Marketing, and IT

Currency Amount

Number Fiscal year Default value (Use calculated value): =YEAR(TODAY)

Table 5.2: Quote columns

Reorder the columns to get the desired result. The following screenshot shows the Quotes

library with the previous columns and a few loaded files:

Figure 5.7: Quotes document library

2. Navigate to the Power Automate maker portal and select the default environment. You

need to create the cloud flows in this environment to make the SharePoint integration work.

3. Once in the Power Automate portal, click My flows on the left pane, and then click New

flow | Instant cloud flow to build an on-demand cloud flow. In the open dialog, set a

name, choose For a selected file in SharePoint, and click Create.

4. The first action that appears acts as a link from our cloud flow to the selected document

library. Click on it to open the configuration pane. Choose your SharePoint site address

and the Quotes library.

filename: Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook_ Build user-friendly apps.pdf
subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Automating Processes with Power Automate122

5. We need to get the actual properties of the file requesting the automation. Click the plus

sign just below the first action to add a new one. On the pane that opens, search for Get

file properties in SharePoint. Set the same site address and library as the previous

action, and select the Id from the result of the last step:

Figure 5.8: Get file properties configuration

6. To create our resulting PDF file, we need to define its name. To do this, we will use the

Compose action to build a formula to generate it. Add this new action, and for Inputs, use

the following expression, using the expression editor:

replace(triggerBody()?['entity']?['fileName'], '.docx', '.pdf')

7. With this formula, we use the same filename but change the extension from Word (.docx)

to PDF (.pdf). To tidy up our cloud flow, let’s rename this action from Compose to PDF

filename by clicking on its title.

8. Now that we have all the metadata, we can start the actual automation. Let’s get the file

content to use in the conversion. Add a new action and search for Get file content in

SharePoint. Set the same site address as before, and for the File Identifier, use the Iden-

tifier collected from the Get file properties action.

9. To convert the file, we will use a feature of the OneDrive/OneDrive for Business connector,

so the first thing we need to do is create the file in OneDrive. Add a new action and search

for Create file in OneDrive/OneDrive for Business (we will use the Business version

from now on). Sign in if this is your first time using this connector. For Folder Path, choose

the root folder or any other folder to hold the temporary file needed for the conversion.

filename: Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook_ Build user-friendly apps.pdf
subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Chapter 5 123

As for the File Name, we will need to set a random name to prevent concurrency issues if

this cloud flow gets executed more than once. We can use a formula for the name, such

as concat(ticks(utcNow()), '.docx'). For File Content, select the result of the pre-

vious step.

10. To do the conversion, we need to add a new action. Search for Convert file in OneDrive

for Business. For File, select the Id of the previous step and set PDF as the Target type.

11. Let’s add a new action to delete our temp file and avoid clutter in our OneDrive. Search

for Delete file in OneDrive for Business. For File, select the Id of the Create file action:

Figure 5.9: OneDrive actions

12. The next step is to get the PDF file back to SharePoint, but before we do, we need to consider

the scenario that this might be a second execution of the cloud flow, so we will need to do

some cleanup first: if the file exists already, let’s delete it. Add a new action, and search

for Get file metadata using path in SharePoint to check whether the PDF file already

exists. Set the same Site Address as before and, in File Path, input /Quotes/. Then, from

the Dynamic Content selector, choose Outputs from the PDF filename action.

13. Add a new action called Delete file in SharePoint. Set the same Site Address as before,

use the Id from the previous step as the input of File Identifier, and rename this action

Delete PDF file:

Figure 5.10: SharePoint actions

filename: Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook_ Build user-friendly apps.pdf
subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides

14. Keep in mind that the first time this cloud flow gets executed, the PDF file won’t exist, so

we need to inform Power Automate that if any of the previous two steps fail, it should

continue to run the rest of the actions. To do this, we will add a new action called Scope.

This action allows us to encapsulate several steps together. If one fails, the entire scope

fails. Rename this action Check for existing file

15. Drag the Get file metadata using path and Delete PDF file actions inside the scope, pre-

serving the same order.

16. Add a new action and search for Create file in SharePoint. Set the same site address

and path as in previous actions. For File Name, use the Outputs from the PDF filename

action, and for File Content, get the conversion result of the Convert file step. Go to the

Settings tab of this action, and under the Run After section, check Has failed. Rename

this action Create PDF file:

Figure 5.11: Run After configuration

17. We now need to replicate the same metadata as the original file. Add a new action and

search for Update file properties in SharePoint. Set the same site address and library

as before, and set the ItemId from the last file creation step as the Id. The rest of the fields

come from the Get file properties result. Remember to click the Show all button to display

all the library columns.

Keep in mind that the Department field is of the Choice type, so we need to use the actual

value by searching for Department Value and entering it as a custom value:

subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides

Chapter 5 125

Figure 5.12: Column metadata replication

18. The last step is to notify the Finance team if a quote is over $100,000. Add a new action

called Condition. Using the action properties, build an expression to check whether the

Amount value of the Get file properties result is greater than $100,000. Rename this

condition Amount value check

19. On the True route, add a new action called Post message in a chat or channel in Micro-

soft Teams. Sign in if this is the first time using this connector in this environment, select

Channel in the Post in field, set the desired Team and Channel, and build a message

using the Get file properties values. Rename this action Post a message to Finance

The following screenshot shows the amount check condition and a notification message

example:

20. Add any action for the False route, but for now, click Save on the toolbar and close the

designer.

How it works…

Returning to the document library, you will notice that if you select a file and click Automate on

the toolbar, you will get your cloud flow listed and ready to process the chosen file. The first execu-

tion will ask permission to use the connectors defined in your cloud flow – in our case, SharePoint,

OneDrive, and Microsoft Teams. Click Continue and then Run flow to start processing the file:

Figure 5.14: Flow activation on a selected file

When the automation is complete, the converted file will appear in the same document library

with the .pdf extension. If the amount is over $100,000, a notification will appear in the Retail

team inside the General channel, alerting them about this quote, which looks like this:

Overcoming Power Apps delegation with Power

Automate

Canvas apps offer a wide range of features. Among them, we can highlight the ability to connect

to multiple data sources simultaneously for a given application. To support this, the platform

applies specific techniques to remain performant. One of these techniques is Delegation.

Delegation is a term used in canvas apps that means the platform delegates the data processing

to the data source, rather than doing it in the application itself. As querying data uses memory

and processing power, the less our application uses, the better. That’s why using data sources that

support delegation is a great idea. To get more insight into this matter, please refer to https://

learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-apps/maker/canvas-apps/delegation-overview.

By default, Power Apps limits the number of records retrieved to 500. Even if your data source

supports delegation, requesting more items will throw a warning because the platform won’t be

able to retrieve all the requested data.

subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides

The following screenshot shows the sign on top of the label that calculates the number of records

of a SharePoint list. The list has 3,000 items, and the app can only count the first 500 received

by the SharePoint connector:

Figure 5.16: Delegation warning for a SharePoint list with 3,000 items

There are times when delegation does not work in our favor. As indicated in Figure 5.16, if we need

to count our data source’s total number of records, we will hit delegation issues sooner or later.

We might have missed this when developing our app, or perhaps our customer demands to dis-

play all data, irrespective of the number of records. For these situations, we can leverage Power

Automate and the strength of the formulas available in Power Apps to solve these issues.

Getting ready

To use this recipe, we need to have a SharePoint list with at least 3,000 items. Please refer to

Chapter 4, Choosing the Right Data Source for Your Applications, to use the cloud flow example that

loads 500 items as a template.

The files needed for this recipe are available through the GitHub repository located at https://

github.com/PacktPublishing/Microsoft-Power-Apps-Cookbook-Third-Edition/tree/main/

Chapter-05#USER.

USER EXPERIENCE ADVICE

When designing your application, the best approach is to work with filtered data. It

makes no sense to throw 3,000 items into a gallery for the user to browse. Refining

by categories, indexed fields, or any other column that lets you work with limited

data sets is the best option.
