How to do it…

1. Go to the Power Automate portal, https://make.powerautomate.com, and create a solu-

tion for this recipe.

2. Let’s prepare environment variables inside the solution to set the SharePoint parameters.

Click on + New | More | Environment variable. Set the Display name to something rel-

evant, such as Delegation-SharePointSite

For the Data Type, select Data source and then SharePoint for the Connector dropdown.

Select an existing connection or create one from the Connection dropdown. For the Pa-

rameter Type, select Site. Finally, click + New site value and set your SharePoint site from

the Current site dropdown.

3. Repeat step 2 to create an environment variable to hold the name of the SharePoint list,

so for this case, select List for the Parameter Type.

4. Now, we are ready to create the cloud flow. Click + New | Automation | Cloud flow | In-

stant. Name it, select When Power Apps calls a flow (V2) as the trigger, and click Create.

5. The first step is to get data from our SharePoint list, filled with 3,000 items. There are

ready-made actions to retrieve this data from this data source, but we will introduce the

SharePoint REST API to acquire these items. Why? A picture is worth a thousand words:

Figure 5.17: Speed comparison between two actions

Imagine your users waiting more than half a minute to get the data; this won’t help your

solution’s adoption.

filename: Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook_ Build user-friendly apps.pdf
subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Automating Processes with Power Automate130

6. Add a new action and search for Send an HTTP request to SharePoint. Set the Site

Address to the environment variable we created in step 2, leave Method as GET, as we are

querying data, and for Uri, enter the following command:

_api/web/lists(guid'')/items?$select=Title&$top=3000

Let’s break this code down:

• _api: The SharePoint endpoint where we will establish the communication.

• web: Methods to access information from a given site.

• lists: The endpoint for list handling methods.

• guid(''): This is where we indicate that it should look for the list we selected in

step 3. Insert the environment variable between the quotes using the dynamic

data selector.

• items: Gets all the list’s items.

• select: A modifier to specify that we only want the Title column.

• top: A modifier to indicate that we want to limit the result to the first 3,000 ele-

ments. Keep in mind that going over 5,000 items requires further tweaking and

pagination.

7. In the Headers section, add these items:

• Key: accept – Value: application/json

• Key: odata – Value: nometadata

nometadata indicates that we don’t want extra metadata information. We do this to clean

as much data from the response as possible, thereby reducing bandwidth and increasing

speed.

8. Querying SharePoint data using this action returns data in JSON format. To understand

this data and use it, we need to parse it. Add a new step and search for Parse JSON. For

Content, select the body of our previous step, and for Schema, click Use sample payload

to generate schema and copy the contents of the schema.json file provided by our GitHub

repository. Another way to get this schema is to run the cloud flow with just the query

action and get the body from the output, as seen in the following screenshot:

subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Chapter 5 131

Figure 5.18: Response output from SharePoint

9. Now, let’s clean up the response even further by using the Select action. This option allows

us to select only the necessary columns from the previously received data.

Add a new action and search for Select. For the From field, use Body value from the

Parse JSON action. In the Map section, set these values:

• Key: Name – Value: Title

Figure 5.19: Select action mapping

subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Automating Processes with Power Automate132

10. To send the response to Power Apps, we only have a handful of data types: Text, Yes/No,

File, Email, Number, and Date. None of these is a complex data type such as an object

or an array. To solve this, we are going to use the Join action. As the name implies, this

action joins an array to a string using a delimiter. Add a new step and search for Join. Use

Output from the Select action in the From field. For the Join with field, use the semicolon.

11. Add a new action and search for Respond to a PowerApp or flow. Click on Add an out-

put, select Text, and use data in the Enter a name field. For the Enter a value to respond

with, select Output from the Join action.

12. From the toolbar, click on Save as draft and then Publish. Close the designer and go back

to the solution.

13. Click on New | App | Canvas app. Name it and choose either the Phone or Tablet layout.

14. Insert a Button, a Label, and a Gallery. Change their visual properties to match your

desired style.

15. From the Power Automate panel on the left, click Add flow and select the cloud flow

you’ve just created from the list.

16. Using the formula bar, change the OnSelect property of the button to the following code:

ClearCollect(

Elements,

ForAll(

Split(

Delegationhelper.Run().data,

";"

),

With(

Match(

Value,

"\{\""Name\""\:\""(?:(?<name>.+))\""\}"

),

{Name: name}

)

)

)

Let’s break down the previous code:

filename: Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook_ Build user-friendly apps.pdf
subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Chapter 5 133

• ClearCollect creates a new collection to hold the data coming from Power Au-

tomate.

• ForAll iterates through the array in parallel threads.

• Split creates an array from the string received from Power Automate by breaking

it, using the semicolon used to join it. Please note that Delegationhelper is the

name of the connected cloud flow. Change it to the name of your cloud flow.

• With executes a regular expression formula using the Match function, exposing

the result to the name variable.

17. Hold Alt and click the button to execute the code and create the collection.

18. Select the gallery control and set its data source to the Elements collection. Adapt the

elements inside this control to display the collected data, using ThisItem.Name as its value.

19. Select the label and set its text property to CountRows(Elements). Counting the elements

of the collection won’t throw the delegation warning, since we have already received the

complete data in the application.

How it works…

After completing the steps, you will have an application just like the following:

Figure 5.20: Delegation example Power App

As you can see, the SharePoint connector can only count the first 500 elements, while Power

Automate handles the whole 3,000.

We take advantage of various actions to get data from our data sources to overcome delegation

issues. Using regular expression is one way to deal with them; you could also use the ParseJSON

function to handle the response from Power Automate or manipulate the received array with

another approach, using the string formulas available in Power Fx.

The code we used to transform the data in Power Apps iterates through the data received from

Power Automate, extracting the fields from each record and collecting the result in the Elements

collection.

The extraction expression looks for patterns that match this example data, {"Name":"Element

2088"}, and then it uses capture groups to extract the fields into one record:

Figure 5.21: Capture groups in regular expressions

For more information regarding this technique, please refer to https://learn.microsoft.

com/en-us/dotnet/standard/base-types/regular-expression-language-quick-

reference#grouping-constructs.

Power Automate is an integration tool at its core, so it’s prepared to handle a large amount of data

without dealing with application responsiveness, user interaction, or adoption. This capability

plays a role in our favor to solve delegation issues.

There’s more…

A setting in Power Apps can bend the limit of 500 records when delegation issues appear, but it

only raises the limit to 2,000.

From Power Apps Studio, click Settings from the main toolbar, and then change the Data row

limit value. This might be another escape route if you can’t solve your delegation issue at the data

source level and your data is under the 2,000-item limit. Again, these are only workarounds for

specific situations; remember that data always grows.

Creating a modular solution with Power Automate

Power Automate is a powerful tool for automating repetitive tasks and addressing business needs

with its wide range of features. For example, you may have created an efficient solution using a

cloud flow that manages multiple tasks with a single click.

As a use case, a marketing department uses an instant cloud flow to take care of multiple activities

using an email address as input. It can:

• Send a pre-built email to that email address

• Save a logging record to a table in Dataverse

• Send a notification to the marketing team in Microsoft Teams, informing them that an

email activity has been completed

What would happen if another department in your company needs the same activities that have

already been created in your solution? One option would be to recreate the same actions in a new

flow, but what about maintenance? If, later on, you need to change something, you would need

to make the change twice.

In this recipe, we will learn how to create modular solutions in Power Automate that let us break

one big solution into pieces, or reuse existing ones to improve your flows’ maintenance and

readability.

Getting ready

To create a modular solution, we need the help of Power Platform Solutions, which lets you pack

several components into a single distribution package. These components include canvas apps,

model-driven apps, cloud flows, Dataverse tables, and more. Please refer to Chapter 1, App Maker

Basics for more information about solutions.

We’ll start with our previous example, Building a file processing automation for SharePoint document

libraries. The idea is to build cloud flows as if they were reusable components in your solution.

Automating applications using desktop flows

Building automation solutions between connected systems is an easy task using Power Automate.

Develop the logic, tie everything together using connectors, and solve your business requirements

using actions in a cloud flow. But what if the systems/components we need to automate don’t

have a native way to connect? What if the integration involves a legacy system without API access

or database connectivity?

filename: Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook_ Build user-friendly apps.pdf
subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Chapter 5 143

RPA aims to solve these questions through UI-based automation. It’s a specific add-on for Power

Automate, which allows you to build steps just like when creating cloud flows, but this time us-

ing UI activities such as opening applications, sending keystrokes, or simulating mouse actions.

This feature also helps solve those repetitive tasks people tend to do every day. Imagine a situation

where you might be working with an ERP system tied to a mainframe, giving you only a console to

communicate with. The business requirement is to transfer all the invoices from the ERP system

to Dynamics 365 Sales. Since the mainframe doesn’t have an API, the only way to get this data is

by sending keystrokes to the console to get the data.

Desktop flows can automate this task by sending predefined commands to repeat the same process

for you, successfully integrating both systems without manual input from a user. It helps with

legacy systems and modern applications, like the ones you use on your web browser.

This recipe will use RPA features to automate the creation of PowerPoint templates for all sessions

at a major tech community event: Bizz Summit ES.

Working with RPA requires using a special Power Automate license called Power Automate Premi-

um, which allows the licensed user to build solutions using this technology. For more information

regarding this, please visit https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/power-platform/products/

power-automate/pricing.

In your Microsoft 365 subscription, you can opt in for a free 1-month trial to thoroughly test these

features. Go to the admin center of your tenant, and under Billing, click on Purchase services,

search for premium, and view the Details of this license. From there, follow the steps after clicking

on Start free trial.

Follow this link for a shortcut to the offer: https://admin.microsoft.com/#/catalog/offer-

details/power-automate-per-user-with-attended-rpa-plan/738E8152-767C-4E17-AE67-

7545C2D2EA67.

Figure 5.29: Run desktop flow action

20. Hit Save draft, click Publish on the main toolbar, and then click Test to try the cloud flow.

How it works…

Once the cloud flow begins, after a couple of seconds, PowerPoint should start executing the tasks

step by step on the destination computer, replacing SESSION NAME and SPEAKER NAME and

then creating a copy of the presentation by performing a Save as operation, setting the name to

Session - and the session title. Finally, PowerPoint will close, and everything will start again for

each record on the Dataverse table.

This recipe is an example of the automation possibilities to run tasks on a destination device

already logged in. You could include even more actions, such as clicking UI elements, running

PowerShell scripts, downloading files from the web, and more. You can even apply conditional

logic with the If, Switch, and Case actions, to name a few.

There’s more…

This recipe has been created to be executed in attended mode, meaning that the destination

computer must be on and logged into. A different license, Power Automate Process, allows the

execution of unattended desktop flows on a target machine with all users signed out. Please visit

this site to see the requirements to make it work: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-

automate/desktop-flows/run-unattended-desktop-flows.

Integrating Google Forms with Dataverse using

Connectors in the Power Platform play a significant role when building solutions that incorporate

services from Microsoft, other companies, or even on-premises systems. As far as other compa-

nies are concered, many connectors (more than 1,200 at the time of writing) allow connectivity

for such services.

In Google’s case, you will find connectors for Calendar, Contacts, Drive, Sheets, and Tasks, but no

connector exists for Google Forms. You can build a custom connector to make this possible, but

handling all the connectivity and security requirements might be challenging.

For this recipe, we will leverage the capabilities of Google’s Apps Script, which is included in

Google Forms. This feature allows you to build JavaScript code with triggers to perform actions.

In this case, we will transfer the form’s data on every submission to a cloud flow endpoint that

sends a message to Microsoft Teams.

premium HTTP trigger. For more information on licensing, please refer to the Preface of this book.

6

Extending the Platform

Power Platform includes several tools and services dedicated to building solutions that help im-

prove organizational procedures. The tools we use to create applications and integrations offer

a range of standard features in their field while leaving room for extensibility.

When building applications, you need to create interfaces that interact with your end users; in

this process, you might need to repeat a set of controls such as headers, menus, loaders, etc. This

task can be tedious as it slows development when a new change is needed.

This chapter will teach us how to speed up the application-building process using components.

These elements allow the creation of small building blocks that focus on a specific task by en-

capsulating a set of controls that can be reused across your application. You will also learn how

to create custom connectors to integrate with data sources using tools your developers already

use, such as Postman. Before diving in, we will cover the user interface guidelines developed by

today’s tech giants, further speeding up the app-building process.

The following recipes, which we will cover in this chapter, are going to define the many ways to

extend the platform:

• User interface guidelines

• Setting up your first canvas app component

• Building a floating action button component

• Creating a vertical navigation component

• Using Power Apps component libraries

• Expanding communications with custom connectors

• Integrating map capabilities into canvas apps

• Extending canvas solutions using Mixed Reality

Technical requirements

Building and using components for Power Apps application development requires no additional

license. However, regarding the custom connector recipe, we will require any of the plans described

in the Preface of this book.

For a more in-depth insight into licensing, please review Chapter 4, Data Sources and the Licensing

Model, to get a better understanding, complete with some real-world examples.

The completed recipes of this chapter are available from our GitHub repository at https://

github.com/PacktPublishing/Microsoft-Power-Apps-Cookbook-Third-Edition/tree/main/

Chapter-06.

User interface guidelines

Designing intuitive applications has become an art form over the years. Initially, developers did

not consider the applications’ usability; they only focused on providing the required functionality.

Since the mobile revolution back in 2007, an app’s design has become as important as its purpose.

Applications that are easier to use are more successful than others with more features. That’s why

all major players in the mobile industry started to define their approaches to user interface design

by creating guidelines for their devices. Toolbars were initially at the bottom and then at the top;

now, they’re back at the bottom again. There have been many iterations due to the changes in

device sizes, screen aspect ratios, and more.

Today’s main guidelines come from Google, Apple, and Microsoft. It doesn’t matter what type

of device it is; there are guidelines for it. The idea is to give app designers and developers cues on

how to design their apps. The approach is to have one unique backend but different interfaces

depending on the mobile ecosystem.

The applications we develop should use cues from these guidelines because users already know

what these designed controls do. Let’s take the floating action button, for example. Its function is

quite well known; it is the main activity in the application. The following screenshot represents

the use of this element in an app:

Chapter 6 155

Figure 6.1: Floating action button in action

This control is just an example of all the definitions you can find in these guidelines. To gather

more ideas from them, refer to these links:

• Google: Material Design:

https://m3.material.io/

• Apple: Human Interface Guidelines: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-

interface-guidelines/

• Microsoft: Fluent Design System:

https://fluent2.microsoft.design/

Besides these links, refer to these books for further information:

• Designing and Prototyping Interfaces with Figma, Second Edition, by Fabio Staiano

• 101 UX Principles, Second Edition, by Will Grant

• Designing Interfaces, Third Edition, by Jenifer Tidwell, Charles Brewer, and Aynne Valencia

Take into account that these guidelines not only cover how we need to design our controls but

also offer specifications for accessibility and content design, to name a few.

Setting up your first canvas app component

After discussing the advantages of using cues from design guidelines, let’s mix this concept using

canvas app components. With the help of this recipe and the others that fall into the components

category, we will recreate some of the most common controls in the design guidelines so you can

reuse them in your apps.

Imagine building a canvas app with 30 screens using the same menu copied over and over. Even-

tually, the business process might require a new option to be included in the menu. You would

have to apply the change to each of your application screens.

As mentioned before, a component encapsulates controls that serve one purpose. Working with

them is like creating a new screen; the designer and the available controls are the same. The dif-

ference lies in the fact that you can set the dimensions to match a specific size.

Going back to the previous example, creating a menu component will allow replicating instances

of this element on every screen while giving you one single place to update it. Once updated, all

screens will reflect the change automatically.

Components also have custom properties that allow communication between them and the

application. Let’s create one from scratch to see these concepts in action.

Using Power Apps component libraries

This chapter shows us the advantages of using components when building and maintaining

applications. We encapsulate controls that work together for one purpose and then reuse them

across our application.

Extending the Platform170

However, if we wanted to use a specific component across several applications, our only resort

would be to export this component and import it manually on each application. This process

breaks maintainability because each application would have an independent copy of the compo-

nent. If we update one component, all others remain unchanged. In fact, exporting and importing

components is a feature that will be retired shortly.

Power Apps component libraries become a solution to this scenario. They act as an independent

library that can hold all the components you want to share across your applications. The best

part is that if you update one from the library, the rest of the applications connected to this li-

brary will get an update notification, so your apps can have well-informed component life cycle

management. It’s the preferred way to distribute components on the platform.

up your first canvas app component.

Expanding communications with custom connectors

At the time of writing, more than 1,200 connectors are available for Power Platform. This number

means that many organizations, besides Microsoft, support using this connectivity solution for

Power Apps, Power Automate, and Logic Apps.

You can find connectors from Adobe, Amazon, Jira, and Google, to name a few. But what happens

if you need to connect to an Application Programming Interface (API) created inside or outside

your organization, or perhaps if you need to go beyond what the Jira connector offers? For these

scenarios, there are custom connectors.

They allow the creation of a set of connection methods for a specific endpoint with the defined

properties. These can then be shared across your organization and even certified by Microsoft to

be available for all Power Apps, Power Automate, and Logic Apps users.

Extending canvas solutions using mixed reality

Mixed reality is a technology that allows us to extend beyond device screens and into our living

spaces.

This skill can bring solutions to different scenarios, such as the following:

• Measuring hard-to-reach areas or distances while adding this information to a data source

• As a medical equipment representative, being able to show the equipment to the hospital

in mixed reality to check for fitting measurements

• Representing furniture in your living room to see if it will fit your style

Canvas apps allow the building of applications for these scenarios using three mixed reality

controls: viewing 3D content, seeing shapes with pre-established dimensions, and performing

measurements using mixed reality.

This recipe will take a more personal approach. We recently discovered that our water heater

was broken. Its location was hard to reach because it was behind the washing machine and the

dryer. It was then that I turned to augmented reality (AR) technology to measure the size of the

water heater from afar so that I could replace it with a new one that would fit in the same place

as the old one.

Getting ready

Using mixed reality technologies requires devices that support AR. Refer to the following links to

verify if your device meets the requirements:

• Apple: https://www.apple.com/augmented-reality

• Google: https://developers.google.com/ar/devices

7

Improving User Experience

The process of creating applications is a complex workflow. You need to analyze requirements,

design data sources, choose tools and platforms, and build the User Interface (UI), among others.

Power Apps, a platform to build applications, is constantly evolving to help app makers create

functional solutions quickly. However, this sometimes means sacrificing an appealing UI. As we

will see in this chapter, improving the user experience of an application involves many aspects,

such as performance, rich features, and UI improvement.

This chapter will show you how to enhance the UI of full-featured applications created from data,

thus promoting their adoption. We will also discover how to improve our application-building

workflow by creating one responsive application that works on mobile and desktop.

As for data, we will leverage the Microsoft Azure Key Vault service to build our application. Azure

is a platform aiming to help organizations meet their business needs with a wide range of cloud

services. We can use Azure to improve user experience by adding extra functionality for the user,

such as by securely saving passwords.

The recipes in this chapter will help us go deeper into these concepts. Note that the second and

third form a two-part recipe that provides a helpful service for users.

It also serves to demonstrate how we can make our app adaptive for desktop and mobile:

• Enhancing the design of our application interfaces

• Building a responsive password manager in Power Apps – setting up the Azure Key Vault

service

• Building a responsive password manager in Power Apps – designing an adaptive appli-

cation

Technical requirements

Depending on the type of connector needed for your data source, you might need a license for your

applications. Standard connectors, such as the one used for SharePoint, don’t require licensing

apart from the existing Microsoft 365 license. However, premium connectors, such as the one

needed for Azure Key Vault, do. Please refer to the book’s Preface for more information about the

licensing requirements.

All the applications we will use as examples in this chapter are available in the GitHub repository:

https://github.com/PacktPublishing/Microsoft-Power-Apps-Cookbook-Third-Edition/

tree/main/Chapter-07

Enhancing the design of our application interfaces

A platform that automatically builds applications is an excellent feature of Power Apps. The

main logic of the application gets created from the data we need to handle. Screens for activities

such as listing records or manipulating data are already defined. This feature also acts as a great

learning resource for app makers new to this platform on how to get things done for these tasks.

However, this doesn’t mean that these ready-made applications achieve high scores in the design

department. Remember that end-users expect appealing UIs for the apps they use.

With the help of this recipe, you will learn how to improve application screens by applying some

design ideas to make them look better. These ideas will help you enhance your applications, like

the one seen in the following figure:

Building a responsive password manager in Power

Apps – setting up the Azure Key Vault service

Password managers are tools created to handle all your credentials from a central location, pro-

tecting them using a primary password and encryption. They can improve the user experience

by saving personal and work-related credentials for services we use every day.

Microsoft Azure offers Key Vault, which provides a “safe” to securely hold credentials and certif-

icates by encrypting this information in hardware security modules. For more information, see

https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/products/key-vault/

Getting ready

We will use the Azure Key Vault connector to access our data source, which is just one in the ev-

er-growing list of connectors available for canvas apps. It will give us the ability to consume secrets

stored in a vault. This recipe will teach you how to set up a key vault in your Azure subscription.

For the most up-to-date quick start on how to deploy a Key Vault, please refer to https://learn.

microsoft.com/en-us/azure/key-vault/secrets/quick-create-portal

As well as the portal, you’ll also find many other ways to interact with Azure.

How to do it…

1. Go to the Azure portal at https://portal.azure.com, log in to your subscription, and

click Create a resource. This action will open Azure Marketplace, where you can browse

all available resources.

2. Search for Key Vault, and when found, click on Create:

Figure 7.6: Key Vault service

3. Select an existing resource group or create a new one. A resource group acts as a container

for your resources.

4. Select a key vault name. Remember that this name must be unique across all of Azure

because this will then be available through the REST API:

https://<key-vault-name>.vault.azure.net/

As an example, I’ve used PowerVault

5. Select the region that is closest to you to get better network performance.

6. Select the Standard pricing tier.

7. Leave all other options as default, click Review + create, and then click on Create after

the validation passes.

8. After a while, the deployment of your resource will be complete. Click on Go to resource

to view your key vault.

The current connector version only allows the consumption of secrets from a vault. We will add

some credentials to our vault so that we can have them accessible from the app we are going to

build, using the following recipe.

Apps – designing an adaptive application

In the previous recipe, we completed setting up an Azure Key Vault instance to hold the secrets

we will consume from our app. The application design will be responsive and adaptable when

running on desktops or mobile devices.

Getting ready

Building a responsive application on any platform requires evaluating some design principles

before making the app. When designing the UI, you must consider the different mediums your

end-users will use to consume the app. You need to address the size and location of the controls

for every device.

In Power Apps, many layout tools can help you build these types of applications. We aim to create

one application that works the same on desktop and mobile devices.

You can find the complete application and the resources needed to build it in our GitHub repo:

https://github.com/PacktPublishing/Microsoft-Power-Apps-Cookbook-Third-Edition/

Power Apps offers many functional controls to build our apps, but these controls also need to

An example is the Date Picker, one of the most controversial-looking controls in its classic form,

which has beautifully evolved into a modern one. However, you can’t change the date format or

text:
8

Power Apps Everywhere

Throughout this book, we have seen how valuable applications developed with Power Apps can

be. Whether using multiple data sources or improving the application-building process through

components, Power Apps allows makers to create solutions quickly and reliably for organizations.

Keep in mind that applications created with this platform are not just accessible through the

Power Apps portal. There are many ways to use them, such as through embedding, desktop ap-

plications, mobile devices, and more.

In this chapter, we will discover all the possible ways to interact with Power Apps through dif-

ferent mediums with the help of the following recipes:

• Discovering applications through Power Apps mobile

• Leveraging modern browsers for Power Apps

• Improving SharePoint document libraries with Power Apps

• Embedding Power Apps in SharePoint pages

• Making Power BI reports interactive with embedded Power Apps

• Working with Power Apps in Microsoft Teams channels

• Integrating Power Apps inside Teams

• Building apps with Dataverse for Teams

Also, refer to Chapter 3, Building from Data with Model-Driven Apps, for another example of appli-

cation embedding in Power Apps.

filename: Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook_ Build user-friendly apps.pdf
subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Power Apps Everywhere212

Technical requirements

The licensing model for this platform depends on the type of connector needed for your data

sources. Standard connectors like the one used for SharePoint don’t require an additional license

besides Microsoft 365, but premium or custom connectors require a Power Apps license. For more

information about the Power Apps licensing model, please refer to the Preface section.

The GitHub repository at https://github.com/PacktPublishing/Microsoft-Power-Apps-

Cookbook-Third-Edition/tree/main/Chapter-08 holds the required files for each recipe.

Discovering applications through Power Apps mobile

This recipe will introduce how to interact with applications created in Power Apps besides using

the maker portal at https://make.powerapps.com.

On mobile devices, the Power Apps application acts as a hub for all your solutions and is available

in the most popular application stores:

• Google Play: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.microsoft.

msapps

• Apple’s App Store: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/power-apps/id1047318566

Once you are logged in, this hub will list all the applications the user can access, whether using

a phone or a tablet device.

This application offers a feature that allows the user to create an individual icon on the device’s

home screen to open a specific application. This feature is called Pin to Home for Android devices

and Add shortcut to Siri for Apple devices. In this recipe, we will learn how to implement it to

help with application adoption and discovery.

How to do it…

1. Install the Power Apps application from your device’s application store and sign in using

your organizational account.

2. From the list of applications, select the three dots next to the application you want to

create an icon for, click Pin to Home on Android devices, and use Add shortcut to Siri on

Apple devices. The following is the Power Apps application on each mobile device platform:

filename: Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook_ Build user-friendly apps.pdf
subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Chapter 8 213

Figure 8.1: Power Apps application on Android (left) and iPhone (right) devices

3. On Android devices, a dialog will open to place the icon automatically or manually in the

location of choice by using drag and drop, as shown in the following screenshot:

Figure 8.2: Android’s Pin to Home dialog

Remember that this image might differ depending on your Android UI layers, such as

Google’s, Samsung’s, or OnePlus’.

filename: Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook_ Build user-friendly apps.pdf
subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Power Apps Everywhere214

4. On Apple devices, the Add shortcut to Siri option will display a dialog confirming the

inclusion of this action to Siri, as shown in the following screenshot:

Figure 8.3: Apple’s Pin to Home dialog

We can apply this shortcut to any application from the Power Apps application hub.

How it works…

The Pin to Home feature in Android adds a standalone icon, bypassing the Power Apps application

by going directly to the desired app.

For Apple, it adds the ability to open the app using Siri. The operating system leverages this

functionality in the native Shortcuts application. From there, you will find the recently created

shortcut. You can also add this shortcut to the home screen. Click the three dots, then the short-

cut’s name, and finally, Add to Home Screen, as shown in the following figure:

filename: Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook_ Build user-friendly apps.pdf
subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Chapter 8 215

Figure 8.4: Shortcut’s Add to Home Screen feature

The Power Apps application also offers the Open at startup feature, which allows you to run the

selected application every time you open Power Apps.

Finally, remember the swipe gestures available on the application list. They’re an excellent short-

cut for sharing and adding to favorites, among other things.

There’s more…

There is a Microsoft Store version of Power Apps that allows for app filtering depending on the

environment, which is not available on other versions; however, it is missing the Pin to Home

feature. Hopefully, this feature will be included in the future.

In the meantime, please refer to the Leveraging modern browsers for Power Apps recipe for an ele-

gant workaround when using Power Apps on desktop systems. For more information, please visit

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-apps/mobile/windows-app-install.

If you rely solely on Dynamics 365 apps, you can access your applications besides the Power Apps

hub. Individual apps exist for Dynamics 365 Sales, Dynamics 365 Business Central, Dynamics

365 Field Service, and Finance and Operations. Head to your specific application store to try

them, depending on the Dynamics 365 license available to your users.

filename: Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook_ Build user-friendly apps.pdf
subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Power Apps Everywhere216

These applications also lack Pin To Home but offer a great way to navigate between apps. They

also provide the nice feature of always executing the last opened app.

Finally, it is also worth mentioning that the platform allows app makers to package canvas apps

as custom-branded Android or iOS apps with the Wrap feature. You can find more information

on this topic here:

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-apps/maker/common/wrap/overview

Leveraging modern browsers for Power Apps

Web browsers are the gateway for almost every online activity. They are not just for browsing

websites anymore; they also serve apps, services, communication, and gaming. They do all this

without the need for independent app installation.

That’s why using a modern browser should be a common-sense rule for everyone; they use the

latest web technologies and, most importantly, are up to date with security fixes.

In this recipe, we will leverage one of the latest features introduced in modern browsers to get

faster access to the apps we create. As mentioned in the previous recipe, this feature will help us

improve application discovery on desktop devices.

Getting ready

This workaround will require a Chromium-based browser like Microsoft Edge, Brave, or Google

Chrome. For more information regarding which browsers use this technology, please refer to

Browsers based on Chromium section at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium).

How to do it…

1. Go to the Power Apps maker portal, https://make.powerapps.com, and from the left pane,

click on Apps to view the list of applications in your environment of choice.

2. Click on the play icon that appears when you hover over the name of any application. This

action will open a new window with the app running.

3. To improve the perception of your application as a standalone solution, click on the ad-

dress section of the browser and include the following text, &hidenavbar=true, as shown

in the following screenshot:

filename: Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook_ Build user-friendly apps.pdf
subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Chapter 8 217

Figure 8.5: Address parameters for the Power Apps player

Adding this parameter will remove the Power Apps branding from the running application. Now,

let’s see how to run our applications as standalone solutions on Microsoft Edge and Google

Chrome.

Microsoft Edge

1. After following steps 1 to 3 in the preceding section, click on the browser’s ellipsis dropdown

and then select Apps | Install this site as an app, as seen in the following screenshot:

Figure 8.6: Installing Power Apps as an app in Microsoft Edge

2. A dialog will open asking for the name of this app. You can also change its icon by clicking

Edit below the Power Apps icon. Leave the name as default or rename it as desired, and

then click Install. Immediately after this, a new window will be created with the appli-

cation running without any browser decoration.

3. A new dialog will appear from the ellipsis drop-down menu, giving you several options

regarding the app’s pin positions and the ability to enable auto-start on device login.

filename: Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook_ Build user-friendly apps.pdf
subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Power Apps Everywhere218

Google Chrome

1. After following steps 1 to 3 in the How to do it… section of this recipe, click on the browser’s

ellipsis dropdown and then select Save and share | Install page as app…, as seen in the

following screenshot:

Figure 8.7: Installing Power Apps as a shortcut in Google Chrome

2. A dialog will open, asking for the shortcut’s name. Leave it as default or rename it as de-

sired, and click Install. Immediately after this, a new window with the application running

without any browser decoration is created. You will also get a notification asking if you

want to pin the application to the taskbar.

On both browsers

1. Resize the window to the desired dimensions. The app window will remember the size

for future executions.

How it works…

Access to your application is now easier than ever; there’s no more need to go to the Power Apps

maker portal or the Office 365 home page. The application can be executed directly like any other

on your system:

filename: Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook_ Build user-friendly apps.pdf
subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Chapter 8 219

Figure 8.8: Power Vault running like a standalone application

You can reuse this technique with any other app in your organization (including model-driven

apps), giving your users faster access to your solutions. Keep in mind that the &hidenavbar=true

parameter doesn’t work on model-driven apps.

There’s more…

Google Chrome also creates a desktop shortcut for apps using this technique. It might be helpful in

other scenarios, such as distributing these shortcuts using an org-wide Group Policy (GPO). This

solution could deploy the specified shortcut on the desktop of all devices used by an organization.

Please refer to this blog for a step-by-step example of this technique:

https://www.prajwaldesai.com/create-desktop-shortcut-using-group-policy-gpo/

filename: Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook_ Build user-friendly apps.pdf
subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Power Apps Everywhere220

Microsoft Edge can also benefit from the GPO solution by using specific policies, especially We-

bAppInstallForceList, which allows the silent installation of apps without user intervention.

Users will not be able to uninstall these apps.

For up-to-date documentation, please refer to https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/

deployedge/microsoft-edge-policies#webappinstallforcelist.

Improving SharePoint document libraries with Power

Apps

In Chapter 2, Building Pixel-Perfect Solutions with Canvas Apps, we discovered the ability to embed

Power Apps in SharePoint lists. This feature opens a wide range of possibilities to handle this data

compared to SharePoint’s standard forms by allowing you to use a full-featured canvas application.

We can also improve SharePoint document libraries. Since they inherit the functionality of Share-

Point lists, the same Power Apps integration applies. However, since the focus is on handling files

instead of items, this integration lacks usability from a user perspective.

This recipe will explain how to improve this integration by using a SharePoint feature called

column formatting. We can change how columns get displayed using JSON code. For more

information, visit the following site:

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sharepoint/dev/declarative-customization/column-

formatting

Getting ready

Since we are using SharePoint as our data source, there are no additional requirements besides

a regular Microsoft 365 license. We will need a document library with some metadata columns

to improve the library’s categorization.

For this recipe, we will need a SharePoint document library with the following columns:

Type Name

Multiple lines of text Excerpt

Text ISBN

Yes/No Available

Table 8.1: Library columns

subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Chapter 8 221

Please refer to Chapter 1, App Maker Basics, for instructions on how to build a document library.

The code needed for the column formatting is available from our GitHub repo at https://

github.com/PacktPublishing/Microsoft-Power-Apps-Cookbook-Third-Edition/tree/main/

Chapter-08.

How to do it…

1. Go to the desired SharePoint site and create a document library named Book Requests.

2. Add files to the library by selecting Upload | Files from the toolbar or by dragging them.

Once the upload is complete, click Edit in grid view to update the file’s metadata in bulk,

like when working with an Excel spreadsheet. Click on Exit grid view when finished.

3. Enter some test book data for each uploaded file, such as the following:

• Excerpt:

"The Volunteer Chronicles" by Albert Castro: A heartwarming tale of a

group of volunteers who come together to transform their community,

discovering friendship and purpose along the way

• ISBN:

202220232024

• Available:

Yes

4. From the toolbar, click Integrate | Power Apps | Customize forms. This action will send

the data structure of the document library to Power Apps to build an app.

5. Once Power Apps Studio completes the app’s creation, you will get a screen called Form-

Screen1 to edit the library’s metadata. Select the SharePointForm1 form control and click

on Edit fields on the right pane.

filename: Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook_ Build user-friendly apps.pdf
subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Power Apps Everywhere222

6. Leave the Excerpt, ISBN, and Available columns on the Fields pane. Remove the rest by

selecting the ellipsis icon on each field and selecting Remove, as seen in the following

screenshot:

Figure 8.9: Remove field option

7. Click + Add field in the Fields pane to add a Thumbnail. Drag the fields to arrange them

in this order: ISBN, Available, Excerpt, and Thumbnail.

8. Expand SharePointForm1 (keep in mind that the number might differ), select the excerpt

text input control named DataCardValue2, and change the Font size to 12, the Mode to

Multiline, all Padding properties to 10, and the Height to 200

9. Select the Thumbnail_DataCard1. From the properties pane on the right, click the Ad-

vanced tab and click Unlock to change properties. Using the formula bar, change the

Height property to Parent.Height - Self.Y

10. Select the DataCardValue1 inside Thumbnail_DataCard1 and delete it. Do the same with

the DataCardSubvalue1.

11. From the + Insert dropdown, select Media | Image. Using the formula bar, change the

Image property to Parent.Default.Value1, the X to 32, and the Width to Parent.Width

- 60. Using the formula bar, change the Height property to Parent.Height - Self.Y -

20. Rename this control to Thumbnail_Img

12. Expand ISBN_DataCard1 and select DataCardValue3 to change the Font size to 12 and

all Padding properties to 10

13. From the toolbar, click on Save and then Publish. On the dialog that appears, select Pub-

lish to SharePoint. Click on Back to SharePoint at the top left, and in the dialog that

appears, click Leave.

filename: Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook_ Build user-friendly apps.pdf

text:
Chapter 8 223

14. Back in the document library, click on + Add column again, select Text, and click Next.

On the pane on the right, name the column Actions, check Use calculated value, enter

="" as the Default value, and click Save.

15. Drag the Actions column just before Name and click on its drop-down arrow to select

Column settings | Format this column, as seen in the following screenshot:

Figure 8.10: Format this column option

On the panel that opens, click on Advanced mode near the bottom. Paste the code found in our

GitHub repo from the ColumnFormat.json file to prepare the action toolbar for each file. When

finished, click Save and then close the pane.

How it works…

Working with Power Apps embedded in document libraries can help your users when they require

more features besides what you get from default SharePoint forms. However, the steps needed to

use these apps are very awkward in the current SharePoint implementation, mainly due to the

need to open the properties pane to view the embedded app.

Right now, there are two ways to achieve this:

• Click on the ellipsis of a file, then select More | Properties | Edit all

• Select a file, click the info pane on the toolbar, and then look for the Edit all link

filename: Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook_ Build user-friendly apps.pdf
subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Power Apps Everywhere224

The following screenshot shows the first way to open the properties pane:

Figure 8.11: Steps to edit properties for a file

With the help of SharePoint column formatting, we have added three action buttons to interact

with the library’s files:

• Eye icon: Default click to open the file inside the library

• Pencil icon: This action acts as a shortcut to open the properties pane and, therefore, the

embedded app

• Trash icon: Clicking on this performs the delete action

Now, we can easily access the application to edit the file properties by clicking the pencil icon,

saving the need to find your way to the properties panel and even selecting the Edit all link since

the Power App already opens the form in edit mode.

We have added the capability to include a file thumbnail for easy identification. Additionally, we

may introduce more features based on our requirements, such as input field validation, cloud

flow integration, and more.

However, it’s important to note that these types of apps are restricted to SharePoint, meaning

that they are not readily accessible from the Power Apps maker portal. They can only be viewed

within the app list of the default environment from the Power Apps admin center.

filename: Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook_ Build user-friendly apps.pdf
subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Chapter 8 225

There’s more…

Using the Actions column to improve the use of embedded apps in document libraries is just an

example of what you can achieve with column formatting. You can enhance the list visualization,

apply color rules depending on columns’ values, and even call a Power Automate cloud flow to

interact with the file that triggered it.

For more examples of this feature, please refer to the SharePoint List Formatting Samples at

https://pnp.github.io/List-Formatting/.

Embedding Power Apps in SharePoint pages

SharePoint pages are the tool of choice when using this platform for content management and

delivery. Using content blocks, called web parts, you can build pages with text, images, videos,

and dynamic content.

One of SharePoint’s content blocks is the Power Apps web part, which allows embedding a canvas

app inside a page for easier access. For more information on web parts, please refer to https://

support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/using-web-parts-on-sharepoint-pages-336e8e92-

3e2d-4298-ae01-d404bbe751e0.

Getting ready

We will need an existing application to use the Power Apps web part. The same rules for executing

applications apply here:

• It needs to be shared with the users that will utilize the application.

• If a license is required to use the app, it will be enforced on the users accessing the Share-

Point page.

• The users must grant the use of any connectors inside the app.

We will use the same application designed in Chapter 7, Improving User Experience, for this recipe.

How to do it…

1. Navigate to the Power Apps maker portal, https://make.powerapps.com, and select the

Apps section on the left pane. Locate the mentioned app from the list, click on its ellipsis

dropdown, and choose Details.

filename: Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook_ Build user-friendly apps.pdf
subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Power Apps Everywhere226

2. When the Details page appears, look for App ID, as seen in the following screenshot:

Figure 8.12: Marketing Emails - Makeover details

3. Copy the App ID Globally Unique Identifier (GUID) and save it to your clipboard.

4. Go to your SharePoint site and open the desired page to set up your app.

filename: Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook_ Build user-friendly apps.pdf
subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Chapter 8 227

5. On the page’s toolbar, click on Edit. Once the page is in edit mode, locate a space to embed

the app and click the plus sign to add a web part, as seen in the following screenshot:

Figure 8.13: Web parts in SharePoint pages

6. Enter PowerApps (without a space) in the Search box and select it from the list.

7. Once the web part is inserted, it will open the properties pane to the right. Paste the col-

lected app ID in the App web link or ID field. The application should appear immediately.

8. Click on Show border if desired. Drag to extend the web part to the appropriate size. De-

pending on the layout and responsiveness of the app, it should fill the web part correctly.

9. Once the changes are complete, click Republish on the page’s toolbar.

filename: Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook_ Build user-friendly apps.pdf
subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Power Apps Everywhere228

How it works…

After following the web part configuration steps, you should have a fully functional application

on your SharePoint page, as seen in the following screenshot:

Figure 8.14: App embedded in a SharePoint page

Embedding a canvas Power App in a SharePoint page can help its discovery by placing it in a shared

location. For example, an ideal place for a vacation request app would be the HR department site.

The Marketing Emails app is just an example. You can embed more complex applications using,

for example, connections to Azure SQL, cloud flows, or any other service.

There’s more…

This feature adds even more value when external users use SharePoint. Suppose your application

doesn’t need to be licensed by a Power Apps plan, and the application gets embedded in a site

page shared with external users. In this case, you are automatically creating a tool for external

users to interact with the organizational assets defined in your application.

An improved version of the Power Apps web part includes more features such as theme awareness,

dynamic data handling, and more. Please refer to this GitHub repository to get it:

https://github.com/pnp/sp-dev-fx-webparts/tree/main/samples/react-enhanced-

powerapps

Please also see this instructional video on how to install it on your tenant:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EFhP4uu0rlo

Chapter 8 229

Making Power BI reports interactive with embedded

Power Apps

Power BI is the definitive reporting tool. It allows the fusion of many data sources to build dash-

boards and reports that aid organizations in getting the knowledge they need from the insight

received from this data.

Being part of Power Platform, we can expect integrations from other tools that compose this

platform. For example, Power BI integrates with Power Automate via alerts. When an alert gets

triggered, a cloud flow can execute notifications depending on the trigger’s data or even record

these alerts in a data source for auditing purposes.

Power Apps allows embedding applications inside reports to extend data visualization or infor-

mation processing, thus improving the interaction with the analytics solution.

Getting ready

This recipe will use Power BI Desktop, the free report design tool. Installing it from the Microsoft

Store is recommended because the system will update it automatically.

As for the data source, we will take advantage of the Azure SQL Database service, which allows

you to use a direct connection instead of importing the data into the report.

To have an Azure SQL database, you will need an Azure subscription. To apply for this and other ser-

vices from the Microsoft Cloud solution, sign up for a free account at https://azure.microsoft.

com/en-us/free/. Please refer to Chapter 1, App Maker Basics for instructions on how to provision

an Azure SQL database.

Regarding Power Apps, since we are using a premium connector, please refer to the Preface section

of this book to get more information about the licensing requirements.

How to do it…

The following steps will help you design a Power BI report with an embedded app.

Installing and configuring Power BI Desktop

1. The following link will open the Power BI Desktop page on the Microsoft Store:

https://apps.microsoft.com/store/detail/power-bi-desktop/9NTXR16HNW1T

2. Install the application and launch it when it finishes.

filename: Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook_ Build user-friendly apps.pdf
subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Power Apps Everywhere230

3. On the startup screen, click the SQL Server icon, and on the dialog that opens, enter your

database’s Server address and Database name. Select DirectQuery for Data Connectivity

mode and then click OK. These settings should appear as in the following screenshot:

Figure 8.15: Azure SQL Database configuration in Power BI

4. The following dialog is where you can set the authentication type. Select the one you’ve

configured for your database.

5. The Navigator dialog will open, displaying the contents of the database. Expand the

database name and select the SalesLT�Product table, then hit Load. The Power BI report

now has the data source configured for the Azure SQL database. You can start designing

your report.

6. From the Data pane on the right, expand the table and select the following fields: Pro-

ductNumber, Name, and ListPrice. These fields will appear in a table visualization, as

seen in the following screenshot:

filename: Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook_ Build user-friendly apps.pdf
subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Chapter 8 231

Figure 8.16: Data source fields visualization in Power BI Desktop

7. Log in using your organization’s credentials by clicking Sign In on the app’s title bar. On

successful login, click the save icon at the beginning of the title bar. Name your report

and click Save.

8. Click Publish on the Home toolbar. From the Publish to Power BI dialog, choose My

workspace and click Select. Click Got it when the process completes.

9. Go to Power BI online, https://app.powerbi.com/, and from the left pane, click Work-

spaces and select My workspace. The list of elements contained in this workspace will

appear. You will find two elements with the same name as your report. One is the actual

report, and the other is the semantic model, which holds all the metadata. Click on the

three dots at the end of the semantic model and choose Settings from the dropdown.

10. On the Settings page, expand Data source credentials and click Edit credentials. Set the

User name and Password as you did on Power BI Desktop and click Sign in. This action

needs to be done once because when you publish your report, the credentials are not

included in this process.

filename: Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook_ Build user-friendly apps.pdf
subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Power Apps Everywhere232

11. Go back to My workspace. This time, click to open the report, and from the toolbar, click

on Edit. Design the report to include the values, and then select the Power Apps icon from

the Visualizations pane on the right. This action will add a visualization that will act as

the container for the embedded app. Select the same fields as in step 12.

12. Once the field configuration is complete, the visualization will change to embed the app.

Select the environment that will host your application and then click Create new. After a

few seconds, Power Apps Studio will open on a new tab already connected to this report.

Building the Power App

1. By default, the integration creates an application with a gallery and the PowerBIIntegra-

tion control, which integrates Power BI and Power Apps.

How it works…

There are two main factors in this recipe, DirectQuery and PowerBIIntegration:

• DirectQuery allows direct connection to the data source. When a data refresh is requested,

Power BI queries the data directly from the data source instead of importing the data for

processing.

• The Power BI integration control (PowerBIIntegration) allows data interaction between

Power BI and Power Apps. The Data property of this control receives a table of the fields

defined in the visualization, as seen in step 5. For this reason, the code in Power Apps

always uses the First function to get the first record of the Data property.

This solution offers a way to update the data directly from the report using an embedded applica-

tion. Using the Refresh method of integration control, we can keep the data up to date in the report.

Working with Power Apps in Microsoft Teams

channels

Microsoft Teams is the central hub of an organization’s content. The platform offers a wide range

of capabilities, including communication, collaboration, and content access.

One of its most valuable aspects is the opportunity to extend its features through customizations.

For example, you can build custom applications, enhance messaging capabilities, build bots,

and embed web content. Power Apps allows the creation of applications integrated within this

collaborative platform.

Getting ready

This recipe will build an app for Microsoft Teams to handle the channels in a given team. To make

this work, the user must have access to a team with proper permission to add and remove apps.

The canvas app will take advantage of the Microsoft Teams integration using the context pa-

rameters available when using an embedded app. For more information, please visit https://

learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-apps/teams/embed-teams-app#use-context-from-teams.

the deployment of a Team through an application.

Getting ready

The Teams service admin role is required to manage the Microsoft Teams admin portal. An ad-

ministrator can grant you this role through the Microsoft 365 admin center: https://admin.

microsoft.com/.

There is a license requirement for the Automatic deployment of Teams section when communicating

with the Graph API, which uses a premium connector. Please refer to the Preface section for more

information regarding licensing.

The same cloud flow communicating with Graph will authenticate to the Microsoft Entra ID

through application permissions defined in an app registration. An administrator can create

this app for you and provide you with the required credentials. For more information about this,

please refer to https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity-platform/permissions-

consent-overview#types-of-permissions.

This recipe will use a Cloud flow to automate Teams deployments. At the time of writing, Power

Automate does not use a new designer when building a cloud flow from a solution. The work-

around is to create it, save it, and then open it again. Please refer to Chapter 5’s Technical require-

ments section for more detailed instructions.

The resources needed to build this recipe are available on our GitHub repository, which is located

at https://github.com/PacktPublishing/Microsoft-Power-Apps-Cookbook-Third-Edition/

Building apps with Dataverse for Teams

Throughout this chapter, there have been many interactions with Microsoft Teams, from embed-

ding tabs to integrating directly into the Teams interface.

Microsoft also offers a way to build apps for this platform by introducing Dataverse for Teams.

This approach allows the creation of applications inside a team that can be used through desktop

and mobile devices. This team acts as an environment, just like the regular environments we have

seen throughout the book.

Dataverse for Teams builds upon the idea of having several components that work together inside

a team environment, including a built-in light version of Dataverse, Power Automate cloud flows,

canvas apps, chatbots, and more. You’ll find more information regarding this topic here: https://

learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-apps/teams/overview-data-platform.

This recipe will create an application using this new approach for building apps for Microsoft

Teams.

Getting ready

The licensing model for Dataverse for Teams is simple: if users can access Teams, they can access

apps created by this platform. As it already includes the data source part, there is no need for

premium data connectors.

Keep in mind that if you need to use a premium connector to access other data sources, you and

your users will require a premium connector. However, if this connection comes from a custom

connector built by API Management, it will be included in the licensing for Dataverse for Teams.

9

Empowering your Applications

with AI Builder

Artificial Intelligence (AI) describes when computers perform tasks such as problem-solving or

learning using capabilities commonly found in intelligent beings. We can use the techniques found

in AI to enhance business processes, seeing as that is our primary task when using Power Platform.

AI Builder is a Power Platform add-on that brings these techniques to the low-code platform

with custom models like document processing and object detection and prebuilt models like

text recognition and language detection. The model type gets chosen depending on the business

problem it aims to solve.

Besides custom and prebuilt models, AI Builder offers capabilities through GPT prompts to help

makers fulfill requirements such as summarizing or creating a response based on received content.

This chapter will use some of these models and prompt capabilities to solve specific business

problems using the following recipes:

• Creating a customer success solution using sentiment analysis

• Building a text recognition system using canvas apps

• Gathering insights from data with the Copilot Answer component

• Using Power Automate to create an invoice classification system

Technical requirements

Regarding licensing, we can use included AI credits from regular Power Apps or Power Automate

Premium licenses. Still, there is another licensing model that is different from the one we have

come to know. A capacity add-on option exists, which can be purchased by an administrator to

be allocated to the environment where AI Builder is required.

subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides

Empowering your Applications with AI Builder264

This add-on includes 1 million service credits. To get a better estimate on using these credits,

Microsoft provides comprehensive documentation regarding capabilities, usage, and monitoring,

among others. Visit this link for more information: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ai-

builder/credit-management#number-of-ai-builder-credits-by-license.

There is also a 30-day trial license that allows the usage of these features without requiring the

capacity add-on or a standalone license. For more information, please refer to https://aka.ms/

tryaibuilder.

You will find the resources from the recipes of this chapter in our GitHub repository at https://

github.com/PacktPublishing/Microsoft-Power-Apps-Cookbook-Third-Edition/tree/main/

Chapter-09.

Creating a customer success solution using sentiment

analysis

Building solutions for business departments is an essential task for Power Platform makers. Our

goal is to find manual procedures that need automation.

In this recipe, we will build an application to help the marketing department prioritize customer

complaints with the help of AI Builder’s sentiment analysis and then use the AIReply capability

to create an appropriate response.

We will mix AI Builder’s prebuilt capabilities to build our solution. A model for the sentiment

analysis and a prompt will help create the response. To get more information about models,

visit https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ai-builder/model-types, and to review available

prompts in AI Builder, please navigate to https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ai-builder/

prebuilt-prompts.

Getting ready

As mentioned in the Technical requirements section of this chapter, we will need to have AI Builder

capacity either through Power Platform licensing, the capacity add-on, or simply by requesting

a trial.

For this recipe, we will need a SharePoint list and a Microsoft form. Please refer to Chapter 1, App

Maker Basics for instructions on how to build them.

How to do it…

This recipe will use a SharePoint list to store the customer complaints and a canvas app to man-

age them.

How it works…

This application serves as a tool for integrating services available from Microsoft 365 and Power

Platform to build a solution that includes AI capabilities into the mix.

When a customer files a complaint through Microsoft Forms, the cloud flow takes the responses

into Dataverse to continue processing the complaints with the help of the canvas app. From there,

we can help the representatives to compose the most proper response based on the complaint.

Regarding AI, the application uses two components: the prebuilt AI model for sentiment anal-

ysis, which orders the list of complaints based on the confidence level received from the model,

and the PowerFx function called AIReply, which helps propose an appropriate response for the

selected complaint.

The complete version of the application should look like the following figure:

The confidence score indicates the accuracy of the analysis, ranging from 0 to 1. This

score is essential for sentiment analysis due to aspects of language that are difficult

to judge accurately, such as double negatives.

Building a text recognition system using canvas apps

Document processing is an excellent tool for the data extraction of structured documents using

a trained model. Such documents can be forms, invoices, quotes, and the like. However, there are

some cases where the required information has no structure.

Text recognition is one of the features available in AI Builder. It processes text from images and

PDF documents.

This recipe will create a solution to analyze photos taken from handwritten records and then

include this information in a Dataverse table for archiving or further analysis.

Using Power Automate to create an invoice

classification system

Dealing with the invoice classification process is a tedious task for the financial department.

Invoices usually come via email with little to no information regarding the provider, amount,

or products involved, leaving no option for the financial staff to open each invoice to categorize

them manually.

We will demonstrate one way to improve this process: creating a SharePoint document library

where the staff can upload invoices without manually opening and reviewing them. A Power

Automate cloud flow will monitor this library. When a new invoice gets uploaded, a trained

Document processing model will extract the required information from these invoices to enrich

its metadata and trigger an approval process, depending on the amount.

Other approaches to enhance this process include the following:

• Monitoring an email account with a Power Automate cloud flow to analyze the invoices

attached to emails and store them in a specific location with the proper metadata

• Using Power Platform data gateways, connect to the on-premises network folder where

the legacy financial system drops the invoices that need classification and storage

These are just some example scenarios that could be improved using Power Platform solutions.

How it works…

As we mentioned at the beginning of this recipe, this cloud flow gets activated whenever a user

uploads a file to the Invoices document library. It then analyzes the file’s content with the help of

the previously trained AI Builder model. The resulting data helps update the document metadata

of the file in the document library.

Using the Power Automate approval feature, we create an approval request with the extracted

recognition needs instead of building one model per invoice format.

Discovering the Power Platform

Admin Center

Building solutions with Power Platform unleashes opportunities for business users to solve their

needs, whether creating a supporting app, orchestrating automation, designing a business intel-

ligence report, or even designing an AI-infused solution using Copilot Studio.

These platform solutions need a robust backend to support their functionality while also providing

the supporting tools and configurations required to manage the platform correctly.

The Power Platform admin center is the central location for managing the backend of all com-

ponents. This chapter will let you discover the essential tools and configurations available from

the Power Platform admin center through the following recipes:

• Managing Power Platform environments

• Gathering Power Platform analytics

• Handling connectors through data policies

Technical requirements

From a security perspective, managing the Power Platform admin center requires at least the

Power Platform admin role. If your organization includes Dynamics 365, this admin access role

also gives you access to the admin center.

However, when a team gets provisioned with Dataverse for Teams in Microsoft Teams, it creates

an environment for it. Users in the owners group can access the environment’s configuration in

the Power Platform admin center.

filename: Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook_ Build user-friendly apps.pdf
subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Discovering the Power Platform Admin Center292

Managing Power Platform environments

Environments are containers of Power Platform components. They include all your solution

components, such as applications, flows, and data. They also serve as a medium to isolate these

components, whether for security reasons or to have independent development environments.

There are different types of environments. Each serves a particular functionality:

• Production: This environment is the one your end users will use when executing your

solutions.

• Sandbox: This type of environment is a testing ground for your solutions. You can reset

it to start from scratch.

• Trial: You can use these environments for rapid feature testing, as they get deleted after

30 days. There is also a subscription-based type focused on enterprise delivery. You can

find more information here: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-platform/

admin/trial-environments.

• Developer: This type of environment is created when an organization user applies for the

Power Apps Developer Plan. You can find more information here: https://www.microsoft.

com/en-us/power-platform/products/power-apps/free.

• Microsoft Teams: This type of environment gets provisioned when a Microsoft Teams user

creates a solution using the Power Apps application (Dataverse for Teams) inside a team.

• Support: Microsoft creates these environments when dealing with a support ticket for

your organization. You can find more information here: https://learn.microsoft.com/

en-us/power-platform/admin/support-environment.

• There is also the (default) environment that gets created automatically for each tenant

with a limited Dataverse database. More information is available here: https://learn.

microsoft.com/en-us/power-platform/admin/environments-overview#power-

platform-environment-types.

filename: Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook_ Build user-friendly apps.pdf
subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides

which, by default, is 1 GB of database capacity. Organizations can increase this by including

subscription capacity entitlements section of the Microsoft Power Apps and Power Automate Licensing

Guide available at https://go.microsoft.com/fwlink/?linkid=2085130.

Gathering Power Platform analytics

Analytics is a vital tool for measuring the performance of a given process. These measures can vary

depending on their target. For example, website analytics offers information about the visitors to

website owners with clear evidence that they might need to improve their infrastructure to handle
