Sharing OneDrive data between tenants

Sharing applications with internal users is a pretty straightforward task. Build the canvas app,

publish it, and share it with specific users, groups, or the entire organization. If your app uses a

data source, it might require more steps. For example, when using Dataverse, you will need to

configure the security roles required to access the tables in your application.

There is also another form of sharing: guest access. You can invite users to your organization by

making them guest users in the Azure Entra ID. For more information on this, go to https://

learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-apps/maker/canvas-apps/share-app-guests.

Once the guest user gets included in the organization, you can share your app using the standard

method. However, not all connectors support guest access because they work by requesting access

to the user’s own tenant.

Let’s take the following scenario as an example:

A maker of the PowerNimbus tenant shares a canvas app using OneDrive for Business with a guest user

of the Contoso tenant. When the Contoso user opens the canvas app, the application will request access to

the OneDrive of the guest user in Contoso. The file used as a data source for tenant PowerNimbus won’t

exist for tenant Contoso.

This recipe will help you discover a workaround to solve the limitation in the previous example.

You can extrapolate this solution to use it with other connectors that don’t support guest access.

The following link provides a list of connectors and how they deal with guest access: https://

learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-apps/maker/canvas-apps/share-app-guests#which-

connectors-create-connections-in-the-resource-tenant-by-default.

Getting ready

en-us/power-apps/maker/canvas-apps/share-app-guests#what-license-must-be-assigned-

How it works…

The application gets the Excel data from OneDrive using two cloud flows:

• Get Excel data requests the data from Excel using the regular connectors, but an HTTP

request triggers it. An HTTP response handles the output.

• Get data from Flow gets the data from the previous cloud flow. It gets activated by the

app, and the output gets sent back to the app.

The context of the connectors comes from the app’s running user. That’s why when a user exe-

cutes an app that uses a connector, the platform requests that the user grant permission to use it.

If we used just one cloud flow, the app would ask permission to get the data from the running

user’s OneDrive on the Contoso tenant, making it impossible to share the file from the Power-

Nimbus tenant, as we discussed at the beginning of this recipe.

Playing with vectors – SVG in canvas apps

Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) is a vector image format that uses an Extensible Markup Lan-

guage (XML) structure. It means that this is a text-based file format containing coordinates that

create an image.

One particular advantage of this format is that the quality is not affected when you change its

dimensions. Being a vector format, it draws the image according to its dimensions. One usage

example is a company logo, where you need to maintain quality, no matter the size, in places

such as business cards, websites, and document templates.

This format provides even more features, like animation or HTML content styling. For the com-

plete documentation, please refer to https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/SVG.

How it works…

SVG images act as a container of many components, such as Cascading Style Sheets (CSS) styles,

vector drawings, and text elements.

By adding the "data:image/svg+xml," prefix to the Image properties, as we did in step 3, we in-

form the image control about the type of image format it will display. Encapsulating the SVG code

inside the EncodeUrl function ensures correct encoding. For more info on this, please visit https://

learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-platform/power-fx/reference/function-encode-decode.

Keep in mind that we can introduce control properties or variables inside the SVG code to make

following is an extract from that code:

<text x='20' y='70' style='font-family: Segoe UI; font-size: 72; font-

weight: 600; text-shadow: 4px 4px 0px #511B5190; fill: #511B51AA;'>" &

Label1.Text & "</text>

Another added value of using SVG images is the file size. Being text-only files, the file size is min-

imal. For comparison purposes, the background image on Screen1 occupies just 474 bytes. If we

used regular formats, such as JPG images, the file size would increase to 10,717 bytes. In the end,

the fewer resources our applications consume, the better.

Screen2, which you can find here: http://samherbert.net/svg-loaders. Just make sure to re-

place double quotes with single quotes before wrapping the code inside the EncodeUrl function.

Transferring SharePoint list apps from one site to

another

SharePoint list apps created with Power Apps improve the standard SharePoint forms by embed-

ding canvas apps into lists or document libraries, taking advantage of Power Apps’s full potential

to handle SharePoint data. However, even though this makes life easier for users, it is not the

same for makers.

By default, you can only customize the form using Power Apps Studio. To get the complete maker

portal experience, you will have to fiddle through the list or document library settings because

these embedded apps are not visible from the list of apps available on the maker’s portal.

To make matters worse, you can’t take advantage of the Export/Import feature. If you build the

application on one SharePoint site and then plan to export it to another site, it won’t work.

With PowerShell’s help, we will learn how to take an exported application package and modify it

so we can import it to the destination site. PowerShell is a scripting language available for almost

every operating system that allows scripts to be executed with the help of code libraries created

for particular scenarios.

Getting ready

How it works…

Exporting a canvas app using the Power Apps maker portal creates a compressed ZIP file with all

end of the import procedure, you can adapt the app for the list.

Updating Azure SQL Server connections in Power

Apps

Building an app using an Azure SQL database is a great approach when creating a solution to

solve a complex business need. This data source provides many advantages, such as the following:

• Views, which can help perform tasks such as data joining and transformations at the

database level

• Stored procedures, which consist of a series of code routines that can be executed in the

database to help with data processing and validation tasks

• Scalability, as you can improve the database engine’s performance on-demand or by

setting a set of rules

These are just some examples of your application’s instant capabilities when using this data source.

filename: Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook_ Build user-friendly apps.pdf
subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Chapter 11 337

When building solutions for the enterprise, using environments such as development, testing, and

production is a good practice. These environments help developers iterate application versions

without affecting end-users daily tasks when using your solution.

However, when using Azure SQL canvas apps, transferring apps between environments is not as

straightforward as it should be. This is because the data source connection is linked to the app.

When you move it to another environment, it remains connected to the development database.

There is no easy way to change it to a production database other than deleting all connections

and adding them again, pointing to the production database.

Getting ready

In this recipe, we will explore a solution to simplify the transfer process using PowerShell. If you

need instructions on how to prepare your device to work with PowerShell, please refer to the

Getting ready section of the Transferring SharePoint list apps from one site to another recipe.

The complete script can be found in our GitHub repository. We will use it with specific parameters

to help us transfer our application.

Azure SQL databases

For this scenario, we will need two databases: one for the development environment and another

for the production environment. Refer to Chapter 1, App Maker Basics, or follow this quick-start

guide to help you build the required databases: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/

azure-sql/database/single-database-create-quickstart?tabs=azure-portal.

How to do it…

will assume the names devDatabase and proDatabase.

We will also need two environments (Dataverse is not required): Development and Production.

If you already have these environments, skip to the Building the app section.

Be sure you select to use sample data when creating the databases.

How it works…

Using the provided script, you can change the connections included in the exported package. It

takes care of the package configuration properties and the included app by replacing the source

connection configuration with the destination one:

• fileName: This is the exported “base” solution.

• sourceServer: This represents the source Azure SQL Server name.

• sourceDatabase: As before, this is the source Azure SQL database name.

• sourceConnectionID: This is the GUID of the source connection.

• destinationServer: This is the destination Azure SQL Server name.

• destinationDatabase: This is the destination Azure SQL database name.

• destinationConnectionID: This is the GUID representation of the destination

connection.

The destination parameters represent the identifiers of the destination Azure SQL Server, data-

base, and connection ID.

The previous example transforms a simple application with just one database connection config-

ured. Complex solutions tend to have multiple connections for each table or view used in the app.

Manually changing them when transferring the app from different environments would be tedious.

You can use this technique not only in different environments of the same tenant but also to

transfer an app you’ve been building in your organization to an external third party. Each time

you complete a milestone, export the app, execute the script on the package, and install it in your

client’s environment.

There’s more...

The transformation script uses a native ZIP file unpack mechanism available in PowerShell. The

Power Platform CLI introduces native capabilities to allow unpacking to a YAML format for im-

proved readability. Besides this, you can do more tasks, such as downloading a canvas app, packing

it, and even deploying it. At the time of writing, these capabilities are in preview. You can find

more information here: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-platform/developer/

cli/reference/canvas.

Renaming files in SharePoint document libraries

SharePoint is the ideal choice for document classification systems. This platform provides a stan-

dard set of metadata properties while allowing us to create custom properties to improve data

categorization.

For example, let’s take a document library to hold company contracts. We can enhance this library

by adding extra columns, such as the contractor’s name, the expiration date, and the department

that requested this contract. Besides using this information for ordering and classification, you

can also act on this data:

• Build a Power Automate cloud flow that sends a Teams notification to a specific depart-

ment warning them about an expiring contract.

• Design dashboards based on this data to understand the number of contracts per con-

tractor or which department requests more contracts.

• Create a Power Apps app to gather data while on the go. This app can even collect signa-

tures for these contracts.

Throughout this book, several recipes use Power Automate to handle SharePoint metadata in

many ways. However, a particular metadata property is not editable by default: the filename.

for extraction, giving them meaningful names from the stored metadata.

grid view from the toolbar to edit data in bulk. The AMPI Currents folder should look

12

Advanced Techniques with

the Power Apps Component

Framework

Low-code platforms offer many possibilities for building applications, focusing on easy-to-learn

languages, ready-to-use solutions, and a robust backend to support almost all business require-

ments.

However, some scenarios might require a component to solve a particular task with tools created

using traditional coding technologies. Thankfully, the Power Platform is open to these approaches

as well, and that’s why we can leverage the advanced techniques of professional development

using the Power Apps Component Framework (PCF).

This framework consists of code components that work just like regular Power Apps components.

Using standard web technologies such as HTML, CSS, and TypeScript paired with extensive frame-

work APIs creates reusable components built in a single solution package.

MONSTERS AHEAD

Through out this book, we have been working closely with the low-code portion

of the Power Platform. This chapter will focus more on the pro-code side by using

well-known web technologies to build a canvas component. Some knowledge of

these technologies will be required to get the most out of this chapter.

filename: Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook_ Build user-friendly apps.pdf
subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides

Advanced Techniques with the Power Apps Component Framework352

To get more information regarding these code components, please visit https://learn.microsoft.

com/en-us/power-apps/developer/component-framework/custom-controls-overview.

Through a series of recipes, we will discover how to build a PCF solution using Font Awesome

resources inside your canvas apps. This service offers an extensive icon library to help in web-

based projects.

These recipes will work together to deliver a complete solution:

• Configuring your development environment

• Setting up Font Awesome

• Creating the project

• Building the application logic

• Deploying the solution

• Testing the component on a canvas app

Technical requirements

When using code components, the licensing requirements depend on the component’s capa -

bilities. If it doesn’t connect to external services or data sources, it will only require a minimum

license of Microsoft 365. On the other hand, connecting external services, including Dataverse

for model-driven components, involves using a Power Apps license.

For more information on this regard, please refer to https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/

power-apps/developer/component-framework/overview#licensing.

The complete code solution is available from our GitHub repository located at https://github.

com/PacktPublishing/Microsoft-Power-Apps-Cookbook-Third-Edition/tree/main/

Chapter-12.

Configuring your development environment

Building code components requires configuring your local development device and, in the case of

canvas apps, your Power Platform environments as well. These configurations involve installing

specific tools to aid in component life cycle management.

The Microsoft Power Platform Command-Line Interface (CLI) is the primary tool for building

the project structure for code components, and it requires several tools to perform its tasks. This

recipe will cover the detailed steps to prepare the CLI installation, separating each tool installa-

tion into different sections.

Getting ready

The required tooling to build PCF projects supports Windows 10/11 or macOS. We will leverage

When choosing a development tool to build these components, you have two options: Visual

Studio (version 2017 or later) or Visual Studio Code (VS Code). I suggest using VS Code because

it is a lightweight editor focused on web technologies.

uration settings to enable PCF use.

Setting up Font Awesome

Font Awesome is a well-known service among web developers that provides a massive variety

of icons and social logos for websites worldwide.

This service provides users with kits to use its features. You can use these kits for different web

projects as they act as containers with specific configurations.

• A Content Delivery Network (CDN) for faster delivery of assets to use in your solutions

• Domain-level security to limit which sites can use your kits

• The ability to create icon subsets to load only the icons you need for your project

How to do it…

How it works…

The kit provides an excellent solution for adjusting the service to the specific requirements of

each project. You can complete the kit’s configuration using the Settings tab, modifying details

such as its name, the pricing tier, and the allowed domains.

Using this approach, you can configure your code component using just the kit’s URL. Later on,

you can make changes to the kit without redeploying modifications to your project.

Creating the project

When working with PCFs, the Power Platform CLI is responsible for creating your component’s

project structure. It also manages the project’s packaging as a Power Platform solution that can

be deployed to your environments.

This command-line tool also performs other tasks, such as the following:

• Managing plug-in projects that harness the event framework of Dataverse

• Handling authentication to deploy solutions to the Power Platform environments directly

from the command line

• Packing and unpacking of canvas apps

Please refer to the official documentation to discover these and other functionalities: https://

learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-platform/developer/cli/introduction.

Getting ready

Let’s continue by building the project structure for our code component and configuring the

project’s manifest. This file defines your component by describing its metadata with information

such as the name, version, properties, or required resources.

For a detailed reference on this file, please refer to https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-

apps/developer/component-framework/manifest-schema-reference/manifest.

We will continue the recipe using VS Code, as it is the ideal editor for this type of project. We will

also mention how to start creating a component using Visual Studio.

How to do it…

1. Open VS Code, and if you don’t have an active terminal console, click Terminal | New

terminal from the menu bar.

use the following instructions to create our path:

FontAwesomePCF and pressing Enter

• Enter the project folder by typing CD repos\FontAwesomePCF and pressing Enter

3. Let’s build the project structure using the Power Platform CLI using the following com-

pac pcf init --namespace PowerNimbus --name FontAwesomeComponent

--template field

You will receive a series of console messages, including warnings, which are safe to ignore.

Building the application logic

Now that we have completed the project structure and manifest configuration, we can start

This file will be the component’s entry point and will be in charge of the control initialization,

event handling, and control removal.

ts file to open it.

private _URL: string;

this._URL = context.parameters.FontAwesome_KitURL.formatted ?

context.parameters.FontAwesome_KitURL.formatted : "";

// Create the request for the Font Awesome Kit

const script = document.createElement("script");

script.id = "FontAwesomeKit";

script.type = "text/javascript";

script.crossOrigin = "anonymous";

// val is the default when debugging

if (this._URL.length > 0 && this._URL != "val") {

How it works…

Through this recipe, we have completed the required application logic to load the Font Awesome

script inside our code component.

From the index.ts file:

• The init function creates the script embedding placeholder in the web page’s header

section serving the component. As Power Apps runs on a browser, it is also considered

a web app.

• The updateView function will trigger when the Font Awesome kit’s URL value gets entered

in the FontAwesome_KitURL property.

The PCF component uses this technique to load the Font Awesome script inside the app.

One important thing to notice is that every modification of the manifest file will need a code com-

pilation using npm run build. This action is required to make the elements of this file available

in our code. An example would be using the FontAwesome_KitURL property in the updateView

function as context.parameters.FontAwesome_KitURL.

We also discovered how to debug our code component using the PCF test environment. This en-

vironment allows the loading of the code components to see how they will react when deployed

to an app using the manifest’s properties.

13

Reaching Beyond the

Organization with Power Pages

Throughout this book, we have learned about the capabilities that Power Apps offers to all kinds

of users of an organization, from low-code makers to pro-code developers. These skills are often

geared toward handling data internally, but what about when an organization needs contribu-

tions from external users? That’s when the latest component of Power Platform comes into play:

Power Pages.

This component enables us to expand the capabilities of Dataverse beyond the organization,

allowing us to provide solutions such as:

• A self-service solution for customers to manage, update, and review their financial data

so that the legal department can build contracts

• A support portal to allow external users to manage their tickets

• An internet presence to offer all company services

Power Pages is the evolution of the previous method for collaborating with external users: Power

Apps portals. It provides enhanced capabilities with a redesigned studio, templates, and site

creation experience. For more information, please visit https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/

power-pages/introduction.

In this chapter, we will extend the help desk solution developed in Chapter 3, Building from Data

with Model-Driven Apps, to allow customers to create support tickets using the following recipes:

• Setting up Power Pages

• Extending the Dataverse solution

Technical requirements

Power Pages uses a particular licensing requirement with a clear differentiation of internal and

external users. For more information, please refer to https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/

power-platform/admin/powerapps-flow-licensing-faq#power-pages.

Regarding the approach of this chapter, as in Chapter 3, the following recipes need to be addressed

in sequence to build a complete help desk solution. For easier access, here’s the link to Chapter 3’s

GitHub repository: https://github.com/PacktPublishing/Microsoft-Power-Apps-Cookbook-

Third-Edition/tree/main/Chapter-13.

Setting up Power Pages

We must use a specific maker portal when creating websites in Power Platform: https://make.

powerpages.microsoft.com. This differs from the regular maker portals since it only covers

website templates and solutions. For everything else, you need to resort to the Power Apps or

Power Automate maker portals.

Getting ready

Since we will be extending the help desk solution from Chapter 3, Building from Data with Mod-

el-Driven Apps, you need to have it deployed in the Power Platform environment of your choice.

You will need to use the same one to build the support portal.

Keep in mind that we won’t be covering the authentication methods that external

users would use to log in to your portal since the appropriate method depends on

the security requirements of the organization using this solution.

Having said that, from my experience, I would recommend using Azure Active Directory

B2C, since it creates a subset of Active Directory to separate your customers from your

regular users. More information can be found here: https://learn.microsoft.com/

en-us/azure/active-directory-b2c/overview.

Configuring user access and security

Building a website to acquire an internet presence is vital for any organization. These websites can

Reaching Beyond the Organization with Power Pages380

Dataverse offers a security model to interact with its data. Power Pages provides another layer,

allowing makers to safeguard certain portal areas. This layer comprises several components,

including authenticated users, web roles, table permissions, and page permissions.

For more information, please visit https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-pages/

security/power-pages-security.

For this recipe, we will take advantage of table permissions for the base tables and related child

tables. These permissions will be associated with authenticated users. We will also cover how to

use code snippets to improve the experience for users not authenticated to the portal.

Getting ready

We will continue extending the help desk solution by exposing the Ticket table to enabled portal

users.

How to do it…

We will approach this recipe in two parts. First, we will configure the table so that only authen-

ticated users can use it. Then, we will secure access to the page by implementing a code snippet

that checks the user’s registration status.

Setting up permissions

1. If you haven’t already done so, open your site from the Power Pages portal, https://make.

powerpages.microsoft.com, by clicking Edit.

2. Click the Security option from the left panel and select Table permissions.

3. From the toolbar, click on New permission and set the following options:

• On the Basic tab, enter Ticket for Name.

• Choose the Ticket table from the Table list.

Contacts table.

• In the Permission to section, check Read, Update, Create, Append, and Append to.

• Under Roles, click on Add roles and check Authenticated Users.

• Click on Save when you’re finished.

Now that the permissions are ready, let’s add a code snippet to check whether a user is registered.

Securing page access

7. Go back to the Pages section and select the Tickets page. Click on the code editor icon

near the top-right corner of the screen, as seen in the following screenshot:

Figure 13.11: Button to open the code editor

text:
Chapter 13 383

8. This action will open an instance of Visual Studio Code for the web, an online version

that is already linked to the Power Pages portal to make code changes to the web page

components.

9. On the open dialog, click Allow to permit the usage of the Power Platform Tools extension.

10. The editor will arrive at the code behind the Tickets page. Include the following code at

the top:

{% if user == Null %}

<script>

window.location.href = './SignIn/';

</script>

{% endif %}

11. Close the VS Code editor and click Sync on the open dialog to merge the code changes

into the page.

How it works…

After setting up the pages to manage the support ticket process, we need to prevent anonymous

users from creating tickets without at least registering on the portal.

First, we secure access to the Ticket table at the Power Pages level, so only authenticated users

can access the records from this table, even if they already know the URL to create tickets or view

their details. We also configured child permissions to tables related to the Ticket table so the data

is available for controls such as the Timeline and the Ticket operations subgrid.

Second, we added custom code to the Tickets page to check for the current user. If we don’t have

one, we redirect to the sign-in/register page.

There’s more…

The code used to redirect users is called Liquid. It’s an open-source template language to create

dynamic content. Please refer to the official documentation to review all the possibilities that this

language provides to add custom template logic to your sites: https://learn.microsoft.com/

en-us/power-pages/configure/liquid/liquid-overview

Liquid is one of the ways to use code components, which we covered in Chapter 12, Advanced

Techniques with the Power Apps Component Framework. More information is available here: https://

learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-pages/configure/liquid/component-framework-liquid

Another approach is to leverage the Power Pages designer and configuration to allow the usage

of code components. Please visit this link to gather more information in this regard: https://

learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-pages/configure/component-framework

Regarding security, make sure you visit the Power Platform admin center and then Resources |

Power Pages sites to review even more features available in the Security tab.

Automating record attributes

Every help desk solution follows a similar process flow. A user logs in to the portal, creates a ticket,

and then interacts with it until it resolves. The idea is that every new ticket gets associated with

the logged-in user, so they can see their status when they log in again.

To accomplish this, we will leverage functionality available from the Power Pages Management.

This application allows the configuration of all Power Pages websites in a specific environment.

It holds every configuration setting you can think of, from the forms you build in the Power Pag-

es editor to the website analytics settings of your provider of choice, such as Microsoft Clarity

(https://clarity.microsoft.com) or Google Analytics (https://analytics.withgoogle.com).

Getting ready

We will access the Power Pages Management application from the Power Pages editor to con-

figure the ticket form metadata. With our site open, we will continue this recipe from the Power

Pages editor.

How to do it…

1. From the left pane of the Power Pages editor, click on the ellipsis and select Power Pages

Management. A new tab will open, displaying the configuration details of the current

website. It is a regular model-driven app that handles the portal’s Dataverse configuration.

2. From this new tab, click on Basic Forms in the Content section of the left pane. You should

see a list of forms available on your site, like the ones in the following screenshot:

interface. Click on it to view its details.

4. Go to the Additional Settings tab and set the following configuration:

• Scroll down to the Associate Current Portal User on Insert section and check the

Associate Current Portal User checkbox. Keep in mind that there is a large section

of whitespace at the top of this page.

• Right of the Portal User Lookup Column field, select Contact (apc_contact) from

the dropdown. Remember that the internal name between parentheses will be

different in your environment.

• When you’re finished, click on Save & Close from the main toolbar.

5. Open the Ticket detail form from the Active Basic Forms list.

6. Go to the Basic Form Metadata tab, click New Basic Form Metadata from the subgrid’s

toolbar, and set the following:

• From its settings, change Create Enabled to true.

• When you’re finished, click on Save & Close from the main toolbar.

7. Repeat step 6, but select Notes from the Type dropdown.

8. Close the Power Pages Management application browser tab and, back in the Power

Pages editor, click on Sync at the top right of the screen.

How it works…

After updating additional settings of the Ticket forms, we accomplished several features:

• Every new ticket gets the current user associated with it. The next time the user visits our

site, they will see their pending tickets.

• Each ticket will display a list of related operations. This way, the user can see what actions

are being made by the support team.

• By including the Timeline control, the user can also interact by creating notes, even with

attachments, to supply more information to the support team about the ticket.

As an example, in the following screenshot, you can see a ticket with all the related information:

Figure 13.13: Ticket details

There’s more…

The Power Pages Management application allows the configuration of many features to improve

the capabilities of your site. Examples can be multi-language support, model-driven charts, and

the setup of HTTP headers.

Adding custom fonts to the portal

The current abilities of Power Pages focus on an easy-to-use platform to build sites connected

to Dataverse. Even though it inherits many features from Power Apps portals, some options are

still unavailable.

One example is the ability to use any font from the ones listed in the Power Pages editor when

making changes to the pages of your site:

Figure 13.14: Available fonts in Power Pages

This recipe will help you overcome this requirement by leveraging the Power Platform CLI and

Visual Studio Code to change the portal contents directly.

Getting ready

We must install the Power Platform CLI and Visual Studio Code to connect directly with our portal

contents. Please refer to Chapter 12, Advanced Techniques with the Power Apps Component Framework,

for step-by-step instructions on installing and configuring these applications.

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-pages/configure/power-platform-cli-

tutorial

How to do it…

We will approach this recipe in three parts: Preparing the local version of the portal, Using preinstalled

fonts, and Using fonts from the Google Fonts repository.

Preparing the local version of the portal

1. Once you have all the requirements completed, execute the following code from a terminal

window inside Visual Studio Code:

pac auth create --environment <environmentURL>

Enter

Note the following about the executed code:

• Replace <environmentURL> with your environment’s URL.

• This action will open a dialog requesting the credentials to access the environment.

• If the action gets completed successfully, you should get a message including the

text Authentication profile created.

2. Enter the following command to get the list of portals in the environment:

pac powerpages list

Enter

From this list, get the Website Id of the portal we will update.

3. Let’s create a folder to download the website by issuing the following command:

md portals

Enter

cd portals

Enter

To get your environment’s URL, go to the Power Pages maker portal, https://

make.powerpages.microsoft.com, click on the gear icon at the top right

of the screen, and then on Session details. You can get the URL from the

Instance url.

filename: Microsoft Power Apps Cookbook_ Build user-friendly apps.pdf
subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides
text:
Chapter 13 389

4. Download the portal to the current folder by entering this command:

pac powerpages download --path . --websiteId <WebSiteId>

--modelVersion 2

Enter

5. Note the following details about this command:

• Change <WebsiteId> to the one gathered in step 2.

• A folder will get created with a name starting with the portal’s name – for example,

ampi-helpdesk-portal---ampi-helpdesk

• modelVersion 2 refers to the enhanced data model used in Power Pages.

6. Enter the folder by entering:

cd <folder-name>

Enter

Change <folder-name> to the folder name created in the previous step.

7. Open Visual Studio Code from this folder by entering this command:

code . -r

8. On the open dialog, click Allow to permit the usage of the Power Platform Tools extension.

Using preinstalled fonts

9. From the Explorer pane inside Visual Studio Code, expand web-files and double-click to

open the portalbasictheme.css file.

10. From the menu, click on Edit | Replace:

• Change:

font-family: Arial;

to:

font-family: "Segoe UI", "Helvetica Neue", Helvetica, Arial,

sans-serif;

• Click the Replace All icon.

11. Click on File | Save from the menu or Ctrl + S to save the file.

subject: Software / Microsoft Power Platform / Power Apps / Cookbooks & Practical Guides

12. From the menu, click on Terminal | New terminal and enter the following code to upload

the changes:

pac powerpages upload --path . --modelVersion 2

Enter

13. Once the process finishes, edit your portal and click on Sync to ensure the changes get

updated.

14. This process works with fonts already installed on users’ devices. Follow the next section

for another approach.

Using fonts from the Google Fonts repository

15. Browse to the Google Fonts website, https://fonts.google.com, and choose the desired

font. As an example, I’ve chosen Finlandica: https://fonts.google.com/specimen/

Finlandica.

16. Click the Get font button and then the <> Get embed code.

17. From the Web tab, click on the @import option and copy the Embed code in the <head>

of your html code.

The following screenshot is an example of setting the Finlandica font:

Figure 13.15: Finlandica Embed code page

step 9 like so:

font-family: Arial;

to:

font-family: 'Finlandica', sans-serif;

at the beginning of the file, just after the comments, as seen in the following screenshot:

Figure 13.16: Finlandica import code

How it works…

Using these workarounds, we can improve the look and feel of our site using preinstalled fonts

or fonts from a repository such as the ones found in Google Fonts.

After applying the changes, the home page should look like the following:

Figure 13.17: Finlandica font applied

Keep in mind that applying any other theme from the Power Pages editor will overwrite the

fonts back.
